The financial planning guide for business owners actively preparing to exit — and determined to get it right. Written by Ed Stubbs, Chartered Financial Planner, Xentum.

Xentum Financial Planning

Cash Out With Confidence

A guide for business owners actively preparing to exit

2025 / 26 Edition

Most exit guides are written for accountants, not for founders. They talk about deal structures and EBITDA multiples and miss the question most business owners actually lie awake thinking about.

Which is: Will this be enough? And what comes next?

This guide is written for founders who are 12–24 months from a sale and want to approach the biggest financial transaction of their lives with clarity, not anxiety. It will not tell you what your business is worth — that is your accountant's job. What it will do is help you understand, probably for the first time, what the sale needs to do for you and your life.

Contents
1The exit nobody fully prepares for
2Getting the timing right
3Know your number — not somebody else's
4The tax landscape in 2025/26
5From offence to defence
6Purpose after the exit
7Protecting your family
8Building your exit team
Chapter 1

The exit nobody fully prepares for

One of the strangest feelings in the world — and one that very few people ever experience — is logging into your bank account and seeing £15,000,000 sitting there. It sounds like a problem most people would love to have. And in many ways, it is. But it comes with its own particular disorientation, one that nobody warns you about.

"You get a few weeks of euphoria. A nice holiday. And then the real questions start coming. I had no idea what to do with the money, whether I'd got enough, or what I was supposed to do with myself."A founder we spoke to, six weeks after completion

The best advice we have ever heard from a founder who sold an eight-figure business? "Do nothing." Sit with it. Decompress. Resist the urge to immediately reinvest, restructure, or reinvent yourself. Give yourself permission to pause. Clarity on the next chapter takes time — but it is worth waiting for.

That said, the work that prevents this disorientation does not start after the sale. It starts now. Long before the deal is on the table. This guide is about that work.

Chapter 2

Are you ready? Getting the timing right

The most common timing mistake business owners make is not leaving it too late. It is convincing themselves that there will be a better moment — a cleaner moment — just around the corner. And so they keep going.

That phrase — removing the risk — is important. Business owners are trained to think about risk as something attached to inaction. But concentrated risk is equally, if not more, dangerous. If more than 75% of your net worth sits in a single private business — one that is not priced daily, one that you cannot sell with a click — you are taking on a level of risk that most people would find difficult to justify rationally.

Signals that the time may be right:

  • You are no longer fighting fires — the business runs without you at the centre of everything
  • There is genuine market demand — you have received unsolicited approaches from buyers
  • Your personal health, energy or priorities have shifted
  • You have not had a holiday in years where you truly switched off
  • The thought of "going again" for another three to five years fills you with exhaustion, not excitement
  • The external environment is changing faster than it used to
  • You have a clear sense that the business has reached a natural inflection point

None of these are definitive. But if three or more resonate with you, the timing conversation is worth having — not with a buyer, but with someone who can help you understand what an exit would actually mean for your life.

The average UK business sale takes around eight months from instruction to completion. Add in the preparation phase and three years is a reasonable horizon for a genuinely well-executed exit. Around three-quarters of business sales that reach Heads of Terms subsequently fall through before completion. The earlier you start preparing, the more control you retain over the outcome.

Chapter 3

Know your number — not somebody else's

Here is something we hear regularly: a business owner has a figure in their head. It is usually a round number. £1m, £3m, £5m, £10m. Or they have based it on what somebody at their golf club sold for. The problem? That number has almost nothing to do with them. It is somebody else's context applied to their life.

The question we help owners answer is not: What will the business sell for? It is: What does the sale need to achieve for your life? Those are very different questions — and answering the second one changes everything about how you approach the first.

Only around one in ten business owners truly knows what is enough for them. The rest guess. And they mostly guess wrong — either overestimating (and holding out for a figure that costs them years), or underestimating (and walking away not knowing if they made a mistake).

The Xentum Enough Number Formula
 Your values, life priorities and the true cost of your desired lifestyle
+An accurate picture of your current assets, income and liabilities
+Evidence-based modelling assumptions (run to age 100)
+The right stress tests: "What if we spend £400k a year? What if it's £700k?"
=Clarity on the sale value that can confidently fund the life you and your family want

We run models to age 100. We stress-test them against different spending levels, market conditions, and life events. We ask: when does the money actually run out? That is the answer that tells you what you really need.

Chapter 4

The tax landscape in 2025/26

Tax planning in the context of a business exit is not a last-minute exercise. The October 2024 Budget introduced the most significant changes to business exit taxation in years, and understanding them is now an urgent priority for anyone planning to sell.

Business Asset Disposal Relief (BADR) — the window is closing:

PeriodBADR Rate (gains up to £1m)Standard CGT Rate
Up to April 202510%24%
2025/26 tax year14%24%
From April 2026 onwards18%24%

If you are a business owner with a SIPP or SSAS, a sale event creates a significant opportunity to maximise pension funding — often the most tax-efficient route available. You can currently contribute up to £60,000 per year through the annual allowance, with unused allowance carried forward from the previous three years.

Business Property Relief (BPR) currently allows shares in qualifying trading companies to pass free of IHT on death. Post-sale, once those shares become cash, that relief disappears. Planning ahead — through trusts, structured gifting strategies, and appropriate life cover — can protect family wealth significantly.

Many of the most effective tax planning strategies need to be implemented well before formal sale negotiations begin. By the time a buyer is in the room, your options reduce significantly.
Chapter 5

From offence to defence

For twenty or thirty years, concentration has been your strategy. You backed yourself. You took risk where others would not. That mindset built your wealth. But it is not the mindset that protects it.

We think about this like a football match. For years you have been playing on the attack. But at some point in the game, you are protecting a lead. The job is no longer to score more goals. It is to make sure you do not lose the ones you have.

When we model post-sale portfolios properly, the answer is often simpler than founders expect. You might only need a 3–4% long-term return to fund everything you want for the rest of your life. That changes the risk you need to take on completely.

"Three years ago my mindset was: push it, chase 10–15% returns through complex structures, keep winning. Now? Simplicity and defence over attack. Do we actually need that level of risk? What return do we really need?"A founder, three years after selling an eight-figure business
Chapter 6

The part nobody talks about: purpose after the exit

Every exit planning conversation eventually gets to the money. Not enough of them get to this part.

We have seen too many founders go from one hundred percent to nothing overnight. And it does not work. Not for most of them. The most resonant line we have encountered — from a financial planner who works with lottery winners — is this: sudden wealth is a test of your existing values. It gives you the opportunity to align yourself, and the time and energy you expend, to what genuinely matters to you.

At our first meeting with every founder, we spend time on the Grab Life Wheel — a life exercise, not a financial one. We ask you to identify the areas of life that genuinely matter, rank them, score your current happiness in each, and describe what a nine or ten out of ten looks like. For couples, the results are almost always different — and the conversation that follows is often one of the most valuable they have had in years.

Our advice to every founder approaching an exit: do the values work before you talk to buyers. Understand what the next thirty years looks like for you and your family. Build the financial model around that picture. Then you walk into buyer conversations knowing exactly what you need from the deal — and what good looks like on the other side.

Chapter 7

Protecting your family: the estate and the people who matter

You will leave your business in one of four ways. You will sell it. You will walk away from it. You will get pushed out. Or you will leave in a box. Most founders have a plan for the first. Very few have a plan for the other three.

Outdated Wills are one of the most common issues we encounter. Post-sale, when your business equity converts to cash, Inheritance Tax planning becomes particularly important — Business Property Relief disappears the moment those shares become cash. Planning needs to happen before that conversion, not after.

From April 2027, unused pension funds and death benefits are expected to be brought within the scope of Inheritance Tax for the first time. If your pension pot forms a significant part of your post-exit wealth, this changes the calculus of estate planning considerably — and it is worth reviewing now.

Chapter 8

Building your exit team — and how to keep them coordinated

One of the biggest structural risks in the exit process: the founder stuck in the middle, acting as translator between their corporate finance adviser, their tax specialist, their lawyers, and their financial planner — each doing excellent work in their own lane, but none of them seeing the full picture.

What we do at Xentum is not replace any of these specialists. It is to act as the quarterback — making sure your tax, legal, and investment advice all serve one joined-up plan. Because the context we have — built over hours of conversation about what matters to you and your family — is context the rest of the deal team cannot always see.

We know whether a deal structured with deferred consideration actually works for your lifestyle needs. We know whether taking shares rather than cash in an acquirer creates a risk profile you are comfortable with. We know what the earn-out period means for your family, your health, and your sense of purpose.

The framework

The Cash Out With Confidence Five Pillars

Five areas where founders consistently need support when approaching a sale. Every pillar has a dedicated playbook written by Ed Stubbs, Chartered Financial Planner.

Pillar 01

When?

Is now the right time? What signals should you look for? What does the market look like for your type of business?

Pillar 02

How Much?

What is your enough number? What does the sale actually need to achieve for your life and your family? Not somebody else's number — yours.

Pillar 03

What Next — Purpose?

What does life look and feel like after the sale? How do you design the next chapter with intention — before the deal is done?

Pillar 04

What Next — Money?

How do you invest the proceeds? What does the shift from offence to defence look like for your portfolio and family finances?

Pillar 05

Family Impact

Wills, IHT planning, gifting, protection. How do you ensure the people you have been building this for are properly looked after?

Playbooks are written by Ed Stubbs, Chartered Financial Planner — Xentum Corporate. Each covers one pillar in depth with frameworks, real client examples, and the questions to ask before you act.

How it works

Three steps from uncertainty to freedom

01

Introduction

The Movement of Clarity — why we wrote this guide

Money shapes every major decision a family makes — yet most people have no clear framework for choosing a financial adviser, understanding fees, or knowing what 'good' advice even looks like.

Xentum's founder, Dominic Baldwin, and his family have experienced bad advice first hand. His father, from a farming background in Cumbria, inherited a significant sum of money at a very young age. When he died in 2004, Dominic uncovered a long trail of poor decisions downstream of thinly veiled sales tactics wrapped up as 'professional guidance'.

His father didn't need a sales pitch. He needed an honest, authentic and genuine guide. And to help him find one, he really needed an unbiased guide to financial advice.

You're likely in the research phase of your journey. We provide these resources to support you on that journey. We know you have many options when it comes to sorting your finances and our goal is simply to help you make the best possible decision — even if that ultimately leads you to work with someone else or to do it yourself.

At Xentum, we believe in complete transparency: honest, plain-English explanations of how the advice industry works, how advisers get paid, where value is created (and where it definitely isn't), what a proper financial plan should include, and how to avoid the most common and costly mistakes.

To emphasise our commitment to this mindset, the final edit of this guide was reviewed using an AI prompt asking specifically whether any sections showed bias towards Xentum's service offering — and unbiased alternatives were suggested where needed.

Chapter 1

What does financial advice really cost?

Buying financial advice is a bit like creating and looking after a garden. You start with a design — deciding what you want to grow and how the space should work. Then everything needs to be planted and set up properly. After that, the garden needs regular care. That's why financial advice is usually priced as a long-term relationship, not a one-off transaction.

The three core components

1
The Financial Plan
Building the blueprint
Gathering financial information, understanding goals, building projections, producing a clear written plan. Typical cost: £2,500–£5,000 for most situations; up to £7,000+ for complex cases (multiple pensions, business interests, decumulation). Some firms absorb planning into their ongoing fee — the cost is embedded elsewhere, not eliminated.
2
Implementation
Putting the plan into action
Opening accounts, moving money, recommending and setting up investments, putting agreed strategies in place. Typical cost: 0.25%–1.0% per year of assets managed. Often charged on an ongoing basis as a percentage of money managed.
3
Ongoing Advice
Keeping the plan relevant
Regular reviews, monitoring, adjusting as life changes, behavioural coaching, keeping everything aligned over time. Typical cost: £2,000–£15,000+ per year as a fixed fee, or 0.5%–1.0% of assets. This is often where the real value lies — but also what people most underestimate.

The four roles behind the scenes

Most confusion in financial advice comes down to one issue — people don't know who does what and what they're paying for. A highly respected accountant we met in 2025 said: "I'm embarrassed — 20 years in professional services and I've never understood this." Understanding these roles prevents hidden or duplicated charges.

1
Financial Adviser / Planner
Helps you understand goals, builds your financial plan, coordinates everything, supports you over time. Acts as your main point of guidance. Works for you.
£1,500–£4,000 one-off + £2,000–£10,000+/yr or ~0.5–1.0% p.a.
2
Custodian / Platform
Holds your investments securely, handles administration, carries out trades, provides statements and tax documents. Keeps your assets safe. Works for you.
~0.15%–0.40% p.a. (often capped at a maximum £ amount)
3
Investment Manager
Looks after how your money is invested within your accounts — decides asset allocation, makes changes over time, monitors performance. Works for adviser and you (if outsourced), or directly for you.
~0.25%–1.0% p.a. depending on whether standard or bespoke
4
Fund Manager
Decides how investments inside a fund are managed. Their choices affect fund performance, but they don't look at your wider situation. Works for all investors in the fund.
~0.05%–0.75% p.a. (built into the fund price, not billed separately)

Note: companies may play more than one role — for example, acting as both custodian and investment manager, or as investment manager and fund manager.

Examples in practice

IFA advised client — Xentum + AJ Bell + Albion + Dimensional & Vanguard

Xentum provides financial advice and builds the plan · AJ Bell acts as platform and custodian, holding assets securely · Albion manages the portfolio, deciding how money is invested · Dimensional & Vanguard manage the underlying funds within the portfolio.

Direct investment management — Rathbones

No financial adviser. Rathbones acts as custodian, investment manager, and selects fund managers. No whole-of-market advice or financial planning.

DIY investing — Hargreaves Lansdown

No adviser. HL holds assets and carries out trades. The individual decides all investments. Fund managers (e.g. BlackRock) manage underlying funds.

Robo-advice — Nutmeg

No human adviser. Nutmeg holds assets, manages investments automatically using pre-built portfolios, and selects underlying fund managers.

Restricted advice — St. James's Place

SJP adviser builds the plan and recommends solutions from SJP's own range only. SJP acts as platform, investment manager, and selects fund managers.

How fee structures shape adviser behaviour

The most common fee model in UK financial advice is a percentage of assets under management (AUM) — around 70% of advisers use this model. It means the adviser's income rises as your invested assets grow, and falls if they shrink.

On the surface, this aligns interests. But it creates some less obvious dynamics:

Where the incentive gets complicated

The adviser may be incentivised to bring more of your wealth under management, even when some of it might be better held elsewhere — paying down a mortgage, investing in property, or keeping more in cash. Managing £2m is not necessarily twice the work of managing £1m, but it costs twice as much.

Where the incentive works well

The adviser is motivated to grow your wealth. Their income is tied to keeping you invested — which usually means discouraging emotional decisions during market falls. This is genuinely valuable behavioural coaching built into the incentive structure.

Fixed fees avoid some of these issues — the adviser charges for the work, not the assets. But fixed fees can feel expensive for people with smaller portfolios, and they don't automatically adjust as complexity increases.

A practical reality check: Two clients, both receiving Level 3 full financial planning from the same firm. Client A has £300,000 — pays £3,000 per year at 1%. Client B has £1,500,000 — pays £15,000 per year at 1%. Is the adviser doing five times the work? Almost certainly not. This is why some firms are moving towards fixed or tiered fee structures. Ask any prospective adviser: "What does my fee actually pay for?" · "Would my fee change if my portfolio rose or fell significantly?" · "Is there a cap or tiered structure?"

Chapter 2

What level of advice do you actually need?

Not everyone needs the same level of financial advice. The right scope depends less on how much money you have, and more on how complex your situation is and how much support you want.

A helpful way to think about this: how many moving parts do I have? And how confident do I feel managing them myself?

0
Level 0
Self-Directed (DIY / Robo)
You open accounts, pick funds, select a risk level, and automate savings via platforms like Hargreaves Lansdown or robo-advisers like Nutmeg. Efficient and low-cost. But no personalised advice, no interpretation of your life plans, no behavioural coaching, and no professional helping you make decisions about your whole financial life. DIY and robo tools cannot tell you how to align money with long-term goals, which tax wrappers to prioritise, how to handle pensions, property, business equity, or family wealth, or how to adjust during market stress or life changes.
1
Level 1
Transactional / Single-Issue Advice
Guidance on one specific decision — should I transfer this old pension? What's the best place for this spare £20,000? No long-term planning, no modelling, no coordination with other parts of your finances, no ongoing partnership. It's the equivalent of calling a gardener to trim one hedge — useful, but limited. Best for: very simple financial needs or one-off clarity on a single decision.
2
Level 2
Financial Advice
Retirement planning, investment strategy, basic tax planning, protection, annual review, light-touch cashflow modelling. Usually investment-led — the conversation often starts with "How should your money be invested?" rather than "What kind of life are you trying to build?" A solid middle ground for managing money well, but not a full life-planning framework. Best for: multiple accounts or pensions; people who value investment discipline and tax awareness.
3
Level 3
Full Financial Planning (Life-Centred)
Starts with your life, not your investments. Detailed cashflow modelling to age 100+, tax strategy and optimisation, family and intergenerational planning, estate and legacy design, business-owner planning, investment strategy built around the plan, behavioural coaching, proactive reviews, coordination with accountants and solicitors. The focus shifts from "Are your finances being managed properly?" to "Is your money supporting the life you want — now and in the future?" Best for: major transitions, business owners, families with complex finances, anyone seeking proactive ongoing relationship.
A useful signal on scope

Reviews are now a significant factor in how AI and Google rank financial advisers. If a firm has a high volume of reviews per adviser, that signals a lower service level — a genuine Level 3 financial planner can only properly serve 50–60 clients maximum per adviser. Advisers with 100+ reviews are likely operating at Level 2, not Level 3. This number may increase with AI, but it's a useful proxy today.

Chapter 3

Which type of financial advice is right for you?

Before choosing the type of advice you need, understand something most consumers never hear: there is no single adviser type who sits neutrally above both property and investment decisions. Property specialists recommend property. Financial advisers recommend portfolios, pensions, and tax wrappers. Understanding this bias matters before you choose.

Property vs portfolio investing

Ratings reflect relative strengths, not superiority. ⭐⭐⭐ = Strong  ·  ⭐⭐ = Moderate  ·  ⭐ = Natural limitation

CriteriaProperty InvestingRatingPortfolio Investing (via Adviser)Rating
LiquiditySlow to buy/sell; high transaction costs⭐Very quick to buy/sell; low transaction costs⭐⭐⭐
DiversificationConcentrated unless holding multiple properties⭐⭐Easily diversified across assets, sectors, regions⭐⭐⭐
LeverageStrong mortgage access, amplifying returns and risks⭐⭐⭐Limited leverage; emphasis on controlled risk⭐⭐
Inflation resilienceRents and values often move with inflation⭐⭐⭐Equities historically outperform inflation; bonds add stability⭐⭐⭐
Upfront costsHigh entry costs (deposit, stamp duty, legal, refurb)⭐Low entry threshold⭐⭐⭐
Ongoing costsMaintenance, repairs, insurance, voids, management fees⭐Low predictable ongoing costs (fund/platform fees)⭐⭐⭐
Volatility experiencePrices change slowly; volatility feels lower⭐⭐Markets fluctuate daily; requires emotional resilience⭐
Control & autonomyHigh: you choose property, tenants, improvements⭐⭐⭐Low: delegated to fund managers and advisers⭐
Tax treatmentSome advantages remain; others tightened in recent years⭐⭐Strong long-term advantages via ISAs and pensions⭐⭐⭐

The four types of advice — and what scopes they can deliver

TypeLevel 1Level 2Level 3Notes
DIY / Self-Directed✗ No✗ No✗ NoTools to invest, not to plan. No human advice relationship, no financial planning.
Robo-Advice⚠ Partial✗ No✗ NoAutomates DIY investing. No tax planning, no retirement design, no property integration. Beware the behaviour gap (1–2% p.a.).
Restricted Advice✓ Yes✓ Yes⚠ SometimesHuman relationship within a specific product set. Product limits may affect complex needs but not necessarily planning.
Independent (IFA)✓ Yes✓ Yes⚠ SometimesWhole-of-market choice. Not all IFAs operate with a full life-centred planning philosophy — some are primarily investment advisers.
The key insight

Full financial planning is a scope, not a firm type. It can be delivered by restricted or independent firms. What matters most is the planning process — not whether the adviser is independent or restricted. DIY and robo cannot offer it. Independence allows broad product choice, but independence alone does not guarantee deep life-centred planning.

Mind the gap: Morningstar's long-term research shows the gap between fund returns and actual investor returns typically ranges from 1%–2% per year — caused by buying after markets rise and selling when they fall. Over 20 years, even a 1.5% annual gap can reduce total wealth by more than 30%. Markets usually work. Staying invested is the hard part. This is where a good adviser adds genuine, measurable value.

Chapter 4

Is your financial setup ready for advice?

Your current financial setup influences both the type of advice you need and how effectively that advice can be delivered. Some situations are straightforward and ready to work with; others require more groundwork before meaningful planning can begin.

1. Complexity — how many moving parts?
Pensions old and new, ISAs and investment accounts, property (residential, buy-to-let, commercial), business ownership or equity, insurance and protection policies, mortgages and lending, cash holdings across multiple banks, trusts, inheritance, or family commitments. The more moving parts, the more likely you need Level 2 or Level 3 integrated advice.
2. Documentation — is everything up to date?
Any adviser must understand what you hold, where it is, what it costs, what it's designed to do, and what terms and guarantees apply. Missing paperwork, old statements, or unclear arrangements don't prevent advice — but they can slow the process and add cost because more investigative work is required.
3. Behaviour — how do you react to money?
Your ability to stay disciplined during volatility, follow a plan, avoid emotional market decisions, and make considered choices rather than reactive ones — all influence the type of support you may need. People who struggle with emotional decisions or who frequently change course often benefit from ongoing advice rather than transactional help. This is the well-documented 'behaviour gap' — the difference between market returns and investor returns.
4. Property vs investments — are you clear on direction?
This is one of the biggest suitability questions and one of the least addressed. No adviser group sits naturally above both property and market investing. If you're undecided between property and portfolio-based investing, you'll likely need a wider planning scope — but be aware of the inherent conflicts of interest on both sides.
5. Life transitions — are you facing a change?
Retirement, a business sale, inheritance, marriage or divorce, career changes, a lottery win, downsizing or relocating. When life changes, financial complexity usually follows. This is where Level 2 or Level 3 planning becomes far more valuable than one-off advice.
Chapter 5

The key components of a financial plan

Financial advice isn't a single product. It's a combination of components — some essential, some optional, some dependent on your life stage or financial complexity. Your plan should include only the components that genuinely support your life — nothing more, nothing less.

#ComponentTypeWhat it covers
1Cashflow ModellingCoreLong-term projections of income, spending, assets, and goals. Answers "Will we have enough?", "When can I retire?", "What if circumstances change?" For many, this is the foundation — it turns broad questions into specific, testable scenarios.
2Investment StrategyCoreNot just what you invest in, but why and how. Risk level, asset allocation, portfolio design, rebalancing approach, cost structure — all built to be appropriate, cost-effective, and sustainable.
3Tax PlanningCoreISAs, pensions, VCT/EIS, capital gains exemptions, dividend allowances, investment bonds, inheritance considerations, business-owner tax wrappers. Using the tax system efficiently is as important as investment returns.
4Retirement PlanningLife-stagePredicting spending needs, drawing income sustainably, deciding between lump sums, flexible drawdown, and annuities, sequencing risk, minimising tax drag on withdrawals.
5Protection PlanningImportantThe base of the planning pyramid. Life cover, income protection, critical illness cover, business continuity cover. Safeguards your plan so one event doesn't destroy everything built above it.
6Property StrategyOften essentialMost people's wealth involves property, yet traditional investment advisers don't sit above both worlds. Hold or sell, downsize or upsize, BTL viability, leverage impact, liquidity considerations.
7Business-Owner PlanningSpecialistExit strategy, remuneration planning, shareholder arrangements, post-exit financial structure. Requires deeper specialist expertise and coordination between advisers and accountants.
8Estate & IntergenerationalValuable for manyWills and structure, inheritance tax considerations and gifting, family investment decisions. Becomes increasingly important with age and complexity.
9Ongoing Review & CoachingHigh valueResearch repeatedly shows a gap between investment returns and investor returns due to timing, emotion, and strategy changes. Ongoing reviews keep you accountable, disciplined during volatility, and adjusted to life changes.
10Professional CoordinationDependentScenario stress-testing, education sessions for children and family meetings, coordination with accountants, solicitors, mortgage advisers, trustees. Ensures planning is joined up, not fragmented.
Chapter 6

How good financial advice is delivered

No matter which advice type you choose, good financial advice follows a structured, transparent process. The depth depends on scope — Level 1 uses a lighter version, Level 3 uses the complete detailed version. Understanding this process gives you a benchmark for assessing any firm: not by reputation or promises, but by the quality and completeness of their advice journey.

  • 1. Discovery — Understanding your goals, priorities, concerns, and decision-making style before discussing products or portfolios. The conversation should start with your life, not your money.
  • 2. Data Gathering — Collecting accurate information on pensions, investments, property, protection, income, spending, and tax position. Missing information doesn't prevent advice — but it slows it and increases risk.
  • 3. Analysis & Modelling — Assessing your situation and testing assumptions through appropriate scenario analysis. For Level 3, this includes detailed long-term cashflow modelling.
  • 4. Strategy Design — Creating a coherent, evidence-based plan aligned with your objectives and constraints. This is where planning separates from selling.
  • 5. Recommendations — Presenting clear, transparent advice with explanations, alternatives, risks, costs, and rationale. No spin, no jargon, no gloss.
  • 6. Implementation — Executing the agreed actions efficiently and accurately, with appropriate coordination. Getting this right matters as much as the advice itself.
  • 7. Ongoing Review — Keeping the plan relevant as life, legislation, markets, or circumstances change. This is not a one-off event — it's a continuing relationship.
  • 8. Communication Standards — Clarity around response times, reporting, review frequency, and your day-to-day points of contact. You should never wonder when you'll next hear from your adviser.
  • 9. Professional Coordination — Alignment with accountants, solicitors, mortgage advisers, or trustees when needed. The best advisers act as the central coordinator, not an island.
Chapter 7

How advisers add value — and where they don't

Adviser value comes in two forms: financial value — measurable in pounds through tax savings, better net returns, and avoiding costly mistakes — and life value — peace of mind, confidence about the future, reduced anxiety, and freedom from admin. Both are real. Both are supported by independent evidence.

The headline numbers

£47,706
Average extra wealth for those who received financial advice vs those who didn't, over a decade. The uplift was 35% for non-affluent households, 24% for affluent. Ongoing advice relationships produced pension pots 50% higher than those who only took advice at the start.
ILC–Royal London "What It's Worth", 2019
1.2%
Annual gap between fund returns and actual investor returns (the behaviour gap). The average investor earned 7.0% per year — about 1.2 percentage points less than their funds' 8.2% return. Investors who traded more captured less. Those using simpler funds captured more.
Morningstar Mind the Gap, 2025
~3%
Value advisers can add per year — not through investment performance, but through specific behaviours: behavioural coaching, tax efficiency, rebalancing discipline, and withdrawal strategy.
Vanguard Adviser's Alpha (UK)
63%
Of people who received financial advice said they felt financially secure and stable — compared with just 48% of those who had not received advice. Ongoing relationships doubled the likelihood of feeling the benefits outweigh costs (38% vs 16%).
Royal London "Feeling the Benefit", 4,000+ UK customers
4×
People with an ongoing adviser relationship were four times more likely to combine healthy finances with a positive money mindset, compared with those who had never used financial advice.
Aegon Financial Wellbeing Research, 10,000+ UK adults
>50%
Of people with £300,000+ in investable assets said the primary benefit of using a financial planner was peace of mind — not performance or tax savings.
Multiple client surveys

The core sources of value — and where advisers don't add it

1. Behavioural coaching (the largest value driver)

Most investors overreact to markets: buying high, selling low, chasing trends, abandoning plans. This behaviour gap costs investors 1–2% per year (Morningstar). A good adviser reduces this by keeping you invested, calm, and consistent during volatile markets.

Where advisers add value: keeping you disciplined and preventing changes based on noise. Where they don't: predicting markets, calling tops and bottoms, or promising returns — because nobody can do this reliably.

2. Asset location & tax structuring

Choosing where to hold investments (pensions, ISAs, taxable accounts) can be as important as choosing the investments themselves. Good tax planning can reduce long-term tax drag, increase net returns, improve withdrawal efficiency, and protect more of your income and gains.

Where they add value: using tax wrappers efficiently, structuring withdrawals, managing allowances. Where they don't: guaranteeing tax outcomes or providing specialised tax advice beyond their remit (that's the accountant's job).

3. Portfolio construction & rebalancing

Systematic, rules-based rebalancing keeps your portfolio aligned to your risk level rather than letting markets dictate your risk over time. Where they add value: evidence-based investment design, avoiding emotional changes. Where they don't: trying to beat the market through stock picking or timing — most advisers cannot do this, and research shows it rarely adds sustainable value.

4. Withdrawal strategy in retirement

How you draw income in retirement can significantly affect how long your money lasts. Prioritising which accounts to draw from, minimising tax drag, managing sequencing risk, designing sustainable withdrawal rates. Where they don't: promising specific retirement income levels regardless of market performance.

5. Estate & intergenerational planning

Helping you structure assets sensibly, identifying IHT exposure, integrating wills, trusts, and planning, coordinating with solicitors. Where they don't: writing wills, drafting trusts, or providing legal advice — this must be handled by a solicitor.

6. Clarity & confidence (the most undervalued benefit)

Many clients come to advisers for something harder to define: reassurance that they're on the right track, structure when everything feels overwhelming, accountability, confidence that they won't run out of money, help making choices as life evolves.

When we ask long-standing clients what they'd miss most if they stopped working with us, the answer is almost never "the investment returns." It's the feeling of having someone in their corner. Sleeping better. Fewer arguments about money. Confidence to make big life decisions — retirement, business sales, property moves — without paralysis. Not having to think about the admin, the paperwork, the tax deadlines, the rebalancing — because someone else is doing it properly.

Adviser value that is often claimed — but doesn't really exist

❌ "We can consistently beat the market" — There is no evidence retail advisers can repeatedly outperform markets. The real value is in closing the retail underperformance gap, not exceeding it.

❌ "Our portfolios are unique" — Most advisers use variations of the same evidence-based investment principles. The differentiator is process, planning, and behaviour support — not portfolio design.

❌ "We can predict what the market will do" — Short-term prediction is statistically impossible. Good advisers focus on discipline, not forecasts.

❌ "Our fees pay for superior performance" — Fees should be aligned with complexity, service, and planning depth — not justified by performance claims no one can guarantee.

Further reading — the evidence behind adviser value

  • Vanguard Adviser's Alpha (UK edition) — Quantifies specific behaviours that add up to ~3% per year in value
  • Morningstar Mind the Gap 2025 — Annual study measuring the gap between fund returns and actual investor returns
  • ILC–Royal London: "What It's Worth" (2019) — Tracked UK households over a decade; found a £47,706 wealth uplift
  • Royal London: "Feeling the Benefit of Financial Advice" — 4,000+ UK customers on the emotional and wellbeing impact of advice
  • Aegon Financial Wellbeing Index — Research across 10,000+ UK adults linking advice to positive mindset and financial health
  • MacDonald et al. (2023) — Accounting & Finance — Academic systematic review covering the full evidence base, financial and non-financial
Chapter 8

Common mistakes people make when starting the process

Before you even get to choosing an adviser, there are a number of common mistakes that can make the financial planning process slower, more stressful, or more expensive than it needs to be.

❌ Avoid

Starting without clear goals or priorities — expecting an adviser to define your objectives for you. As Seneca said: "If one does not know to which port one is sailing, no wind is favorable."

✓ Do instead

Spend time reflecting on what you want your future to look like — what financial freedom means to you, what timeframe matters most, what you're really trying to achieve.

❌ Avoid

Focusing too early on products — jumping straight to "which pension is best?" or "which ISA should I use?" Products are simply tools. Good planning begins with design, not tools.

✓ Do instead

Start with life planning, strategy, and priorities before thinking about structures. The plan comes before the product.

❌ Avoid

Handing over partial or outdated information. Missing documents, old statements, forgotten accounts — all slow everything down and increase the risk of unsuitable advice.

✓ Do instead

Gather complete, current records before the planning process begins. Even if you're not sure something is relevant, bring it — let the adviser decide.

❌ Avoid

Thinking financial planning is something you "complete" — a single meeting or report. Your financial world changes, tax rules change, markets move, and your goals evolve.

✓ Do instead

View planning as ongoing maintenance — the way a garden stays healthy over time. The plan is a living document, not a document delivered once and filed.

❌ Avoid

Focusing only on investments and pensions while excluding property, business interests, cash reserves, family commitments, and tax exposures. Financial planning is interconnected — missing pieces distort the outcome.

✓ Do instead

Prepare to discuss your whole financial world. The more complete the picture, the more useful the advice.

❌ Avoid

Ignoring emotional factors. People often underestimate how they react to volatility, how comfortable they are with risk, how stress influences decisions. Planning isn't just numbers.

✓ Do instead

Be open about your behaviours, fears, and preferences. An adviser who understands how you actually react to money can help you far more than one who only knows your portfolio.

❌ Avoid

Treating financial planning as separate from the rest of life. Your finances interact with career decisions, family dynamics, health, property, business choices, future hopes, and fears.

✓ Do instead

See financial planning as a life-planning framework that supports better decisions across the whole picture. Bring your life to the conversation, not just your numbers.

Chapter 9

Finding the right guide

A financial adviser isn't just someone who sets up accounts or builds portfolios. They're someone you trust with decisions that affect your children, your future stability, and your long-term wellbeing.

A story about Darcey, a surgeon, and the importance of the right expert

Dominic's daughter, Darcey, needed a significant medical procedure. Not life-threatening, but significant enough that it created worry — the kind of situation where every parent wants absolute reassurance that they're placing their child in the safest hands possible.

In the build-up, Dominic met multiple professionals. Some were confident. Some were vague. Some seemed rushed. Some sounded certain but couldn't answer basic questions without circling back to vague platitudes.

And then there was the surgeon who changed everything. He didn't start with a sales pitch or promises. He started with questions — clear, detailed, thoughtful questions that showed he was building a full picture before offering a view. He explained the procedure calmly, transparently, and without pressure. He described the risks without minimising them, the benefits without exaggeration, and the alternatives without defensiveness.

"Trust doesn't come from confidence. It comes from clarity, competence, and honesty."Dominic Baldwin, Founder — Xentum

That surgeon didn't just treat Darcey — he gave the whole family peace of mind. He didn't try and persuade; he built genuine trust through authenticity, honesty, and by listening closely. This is what the right financial adviser should feel like. Not someone selling reassurance, but someone earning it.

Seven signs you've found the right adviser

1. They start with you, not themselves
They begin by understanding your life, goals, concerns, and values — not your products or portfolio. The wrong adviser jumps straight to solutions. The right adviser builds understanding before offering any.
2. They are transparent, even when it's uncomfortable
They explain the limits of what they can do, the risks, the trade-offs, the full cost, and the reasoning behind recommendations. No spin. No jargon. No gloss.
3. They listen more than they talk
Good advisers ask thoughtful questions. Great advisers ask better questions than you expected. If you leave the first meeting feeling truly heard, that's a strong signal you're with the right guide.
4. They demonstrate their process clearly
You shouldn't have to guess how they work, how often you'll review things, what technology they use, how they coordinate with other professionals, or what happens when your circumstances change. If they can't articulate their process simply, the process probably doesn't exist.
5. They avoid predictions and promises
They won't claim to beat the market, avoid downturns, or guarantee outcomes. They focus on what can be controlled — discipline, structure, behaviour, tax efficiency, and long-term alignment.
6. They talk about your life, not their products
The wrong adviser talks about portfolios, funds, past performance, and 'solutions'. The right adviser talks about your future, your fears, your family, your options, your decisions, and your purpose. Financial planning is about life first, money second.
7. They are happy to say "we're not the right fit"
The wrong adviser tries to win every client. The right adviser only works with clients they can genuinely help. If an adviser recommends a different firm because they believe it's better for you, that is one of the strongest marks of integrity in this industry.

Practical checks before choosing

  • Are they regulated? Check the FCA register at register.fca.org.uk before you do anything else
  • Are they independent or restricted — and can they clearly explain why that's right for you?
  • What do their existing clients say — on VouchedFor, Google, or Unbiased? And how many reviews per adviser do they have?
  • Can they clearly explain their full fee structure, including all external costs?
  • Do they have a specialist planning process, or do they primarily sell and manage investments?
  • Are they willing to refer you elsewhere if they're not the right fit?
  • Do they work with specialists — accountants, solicitors — and can they explain how?

How we think about fees

Our fee model. Why it exists. What it isn't.

We charge fixed and tiered fees. Not because fixed fees are inherently superior to percentage-based fees — they aren't — but because they represent a genuine structural alternative that works well for the clients we serve.

The honest picture is more nuanced than most firms admit. Part of the value of financial advice is proportionate to the assets involved. Part isn't. Understanding both is essential to understanding why we charge the way we do.

We are not the cheapest option. We are a high-quality premium alternative with a different, cleaner pricing structure. Chartered Financial Planners, independent, using the best available technology and investment research. The service justifies the fee.

Why fixed fees — honestly
✓Cost certainty. You know what you'll pay, year on year. Our fees rise with CPI — not with market returns.
✓Reduced conflicts of interest. Because our fees aren't a direct percentage of your invested assets, we have fewer structural reasons to keep more of your money invested than your situation actually warrants. Read how we manage conflicts →
✓Complexity-based pricing. Fees better reflect the work involved and the value we create.
→It's not always cheaper. At lower asset levels, a fixed fee can be higher than 0.5% AUM. We're transparent about this — and we're comfortable targeting the clients where our model is genuinely better value.
The proportionate case — what the evidence says

Vanguard's Adviser's Alpha research — one of the most cited studies in financial planning — quantifies the value a good investment adviser adds. The study identifies specific adviser behaviours that together add up to up to 3% per year in net value. These include:

Investor coaching
1.5%
Preventing emotional decisions during market falls — the largest single driver of adviser value
Tax & withdrawal strategy
1.1%
Asset location, tax wrapper use, and sustainable withdrawal sequencing combined
Portfolio rebalancing
0.48%
Systematic rebalancing versus letting drift affect risk exposure over time
Low-cost investing
0.44%
Selecting cost-efficient funds and platforms that compound favourably over decades

The proportionate point: These benefits are largely proportionate to the portfolio they're applied to. Behavioural coaching that prevents a 10% panic-sell on a £2m portfolio saves £200,000. The same coaching on a £100k portfolio saves £10,000. This is why a proportion of adviser value genuinely does scale with assets — and why a percentage model isn't entirely without logic.

But the intangible value doesn't scale: Peace of mind, clarity about big decisions, confidence in retirement, fewer arguments about money — these are equally valuable whether your portfolio is £500k or £5m. A fee structure that charges purely on assets captures one dimension of value and ignores the other entirely. It also creates a direct conflict of interest — an adviser paid a percentage of invested assets has a structural incentive to keep more of your money invested, even when that may not serve you best. That conflict must be named, not quietly accepted.

Starts with your life, not your investments. Discovery conversations focus on your goals, values, and priorities — not products. Money is the tool; your life is the plan. We use our Grab Life Wheel → to help clients articulate what really matters before any financial conversation begins.

Vanguard: Quantifying the Adviser's Alpha in the UK (2024). Read the research →
The proportionate value

Behavioural coaching, tax structuring, rebalancing discipline, withdrawal strategy. Each of these benefits scales with the portfolio they're applied to. Vanguard puts this at up to 3% per year in net value.

The intangible value

63% of advised clients feel financially secure vs 48% without advice (Royal London). Advised clients are less anxious, sleep better, make better decisions. These benefits don't scale with portfolio size.

Our position

A fee based purely on assets captures one dimension and ignores the other. Our model prices the work — with a tier structure that rises with complexity, not market returns. For the clients we serve, this is a clear and clean structure.

What we are — and aren't

We are Chartered Financial Planners — a status held by fewer than 15% of UK advice firms. We work independently across the whole market. We use Voyant for cashflow modelling and hold our advisers to standards that the best firms in the country would recognise. We are not cheap. We are not positioning ourselves as a low-cost disruptor. We are a high-quality financial planning firm with a pricing structure that is clean, transparent, complexity-based, and better aligned with the interests of the clients we serve — in line with why Xentum was set up.

Story 01 · Inertia & cash drag
Part one

The knowledge trap

On paper, this couple had no business being financially adrift. She is a trained tax lawyer who worked in commercial law for decades. Her husband is a partner in a law firm, specialising in pensions. Their combined professional proximity to money, tax, and financial structures is considerable.

And yet.

"I did my tax return last night, and I was like, I couldn't understand any of this."
The client, on the call

She joked that they had "the worst possible pension" — a pensions lawyer and a tax lawyer, with £500k across their pensions at 49. She knew it wasn't right. She just hadn't done anything about it.

This is one of the most important things a financial plan reveals: professional knowledge and personal financial action are not the same thing. Knowing what you should do and actually doing it are separated by something harder to name — inertia, anxiety, competing priorities, the fact that your own money feels different from a client's.

A good adviser bridges that gap. Not by knowing more than you, but by making it impossible not to act.

An honest observation

We'd be curious to look at the personal financial positions of a lot of professional advisers — accountants, solicitors, even some financial planners — and ask the same question. Knowing the rules and applying them to your own life are not the same thing. Proximity to financial expertise is not the same as having a plan. The cobbler's children, as they say, rarely have the best shoes.

Part two

The real cost of doing nothing

£500kin pensions
£300kin ISAs
~£1.5min cash savings

Around £1.5 million was sitting in cash — money she described moving between savings accounts chasing interest rates, only to find herself locked in when rates moved. She had planned the previous year to invest in Vanguard funds. She and her husband had talked about it at length. Then they talked themselves out of it.

"We've just been really bad with our money."
The client, opening the call

She said it almost as an aside. But it is worth sitting with the actual numbers behind that sentence.

Cash savings rate ~4.5% Approximate best-buy rate, 2024–25. Taxable above PSA.
Diversified portfolio ~7–8% Long-run annualised return, globally diversified equity/bond mix. Before tax, after costs.
Over 25 years, the difference on £1.5m between 4.5% in cash and 7.5% invested is over £3.5 million in foregone growth. That is the real cost of inertia — not a fee, but a decision not taken.

She didn't push back on that. She knew it was true. What she had lacked wasn't knowledge — it was the structure to convert knowledge into action. The gap between intention and implementation is where the value of an adviser lives.

Part three

The retirement question they couldn't answer

"I don't really want it beyond this year. But he's like, well, until we know our financial position, we can't make that decision."
The client, on the conversation she and her husband keep having

This is the question that sits underneath almost every conversation we have with families at this stage of life. Not "where should we invest?" but "can he actually stop?" And without a plan, neither of them could answer it. So he kept working. And the conversation kept happening.

A WealthPlan™ answers that question with a number — built from 50 years of modelled income, spending, assets, tax, inflation, and every what-if scenario a family might face. It doesn't tell you what to decide. It gives you the information to decide with confidence, rather than anxiety.

For a partner at a law firm approaching 50, the difference between "we think we probably have enough" and "we know we have enough" can be years of unnecessary work.

Part four

Life doesn't stay still

Getting the initial plan right is the foundation. But the reason ongoing advice has genuine, lasting value is not about monitoring portfolios. It is about what happens next — because something always does.

For this couple alone, the foreseeable changes over the next decade include:

  • Her return to work — uncertain timing, uncertain income, material impact on their tax position and spending model
  • Two children reaching university age within three years of each other — costs, timing, and whether to fund property purchases afterwards
  • Her husband's potential step-back from the partnership — triggering pension decisions, equity release from the firm, and a fundamental change in their income structure
  • Ageing parents — potential inheritance, potential care costs, and restructuring their own estate planning in response
  • Investment markets doing what they always do — moving, sometimes sharply, in ways that test resolve and invite bad decisions

Each of these moments is a fork in the road. The value of an adviser is not that they predict what happens. It is that when something does happen, there is someone already embedded in your full picture who can tell you what it means and what to do next.

The long view

A financial plan built today is a snapshot. An adviser relationship built over time is something different — it is someone who has seen your life evolve, who knows where the money is and why, and who is there at every decision point to help you think clearly rather than react emotionally.

That is the real value. Not the plan. The person.

Part five

What changed by the end of the call

She came in thinking about a one-off consultancy engagement. She left having understood the three-stage model — and having lost most of her active resistance to ongoing guidance.

"So kind of like three parts then. There's the plan, there's the implementation... and then there's the ongoing kind of management."
The client, summarising what she'd understood

More telling was what she stopped saying. At the start of the call, she was explicit that they didn't need ongoing management. By the end, she wasn't making that argument anymore.

What shifted wasn't a sales technique. It was the gradual exposure of the gap between her opening position — "I'll implement it myself" — and what the evidence of her own behaviour actually showed. A couple with over two million pounds in assets, who had spent a year planning to invest and hadn't. A pensions lawyer who hadn't optimised their pension. A tax lawyer who struggled with her own tax return the night before.

She didn't need more information. She needed accountability, structure, and someone to make the first step feel safe enough to take. That is what a good adviser provides — not just in the plan, but at every financial crossroads in the decades that follow.

Recognise any of this?

Story 02 · The quality question
The questionDIY vs professional advice
The real issueKnowledge gap + execution gap
The honest answerQuality costs more. That's fair.
Part one

The knowledge problem — and why it's not what you think it is

There's a version of this conversation that goes: "I'm reasonably financially literate. I understand ISAs, I know what a pension is, I can use a spreadsheet. Why do I need to pay someone else to do this?"

It's a fair question. And it deserves a fair answer — not a sales pitch.

Think about Pat, who is having a new kitchen fitted. Pat is not going to manufacture her own cabinets. She doesn't have the equipment, the materials, or the skills. More importantly, she's not going to try, because she'd make an absolute mess of it — and she knows it.

But here's the part that really matters: even once Pat has the right kitchen — the right units, the right appliances, the right specification for what she actually wants — she still can't fit it herself. She needs someone to install it correctly. Someone who does this every day. Someone who knows where the problems come, how to handle the unexpected, and how to make it look exactly right when it's done.

Financial planning has the same structure. There's the knowledge of what you need. There's the sourcing of the right products. And then there's the execution — the actual fitting — which is where most people underestimate how much can go wrong.
The two gaps most people don't account for

What most people discover — sometimes expensively — is that there are actually two gaps. The knowledge gap is the one they expect. The execution gap is the one that catches them. They understand, in principle, that they should be investing tax-efficiently, planning their pension withdrawals carefully, structuring their protection correctly. What they can't do is actually get it done, in the right order, in the right wrappers, with the right providers, at the right time.

The Morningstar behavioural gap

Morningstar's research consistently finds that the average investor earns significantly less than the funds they invest in — because they buy after markets rise and sell after they fall. The gap between what funds return and what investors actually receive has been measured at around 1.7% per year. That's not a fee. That's a self-inflicted cost of managing money without structure, without accountability, and without someone to talk you out of the decisions you'll regret.

Part two

The choice of fitter — and why it matters more than the kitchen

So Pat has accepted she needs someone to fit her kitchen. Now she has a choice.

She can call John, who she knows from the tennis club. John does a kitchen fit maybe once a year. He's a decent guy. He's not expensive. He doesn't have testimonials because he hasn't done enough of them to accumulate any. And he'll probably do a reasonable job — assuming nothing unexpected comes up.

Or she can hire the A team. The firm that does this every day. The team that has done hundreds of kitchen fits, has a long list of five-star reviews, charges accordingly, and will handle every complication without missing a step. They cost more. They cost more because they're better. That's not a moral failing — it's how markets work when quality has a track record.

At no point does anyone say that the company providing the best quality service and charging higher fees for it is somehow taking money from you. You've just paid for a better job.
The ethics of charging for quality

This is the point that tends to get obscured in conversations about financial advice fees: charging well for a high-quality service that delivers genuine value is not exploitative. It's honest commerce.

At no point, when Pat looks at her finished kitchen and thinks "I'm really happy with that — that's going to be right for the next 20 years", does she feel that she was taken advantage of because she has less money in her bank account than she did before. She valued the quality of the job. She paid for the quality of the job. That's the entire transaction.

What would actually be unethical is charging a premium and delivering John's level of service. Or charging John's rates while knowing you're not equipped to do the job properly. Both happen in financial services. Neither should.

Part three

The thing people say they'll do — and the thing they actually do

The most common objection to ongoing financial planning isn't cost. It's confidence. "I'll keep an eye on it myself. If something changes, I'll deal with it."

Life doesn't cooperate with that plan. Markets move. Tax rules change. Circumstances shift — careers, relationships, health, inheritance. And when those things happen, they tend to happen all at once, or at the worst possible moment, or at a moment when you're also dealing with something else entirely and the last thing you have bandwidth for is reviewing your pension drawdown strategy.

The honest truth is that life just passes by. People don't carve out the time to actually sit down with their financial position and do something with it — not because they're lazy or irresponsible, but because they're busy and their life is full of other demands that feel more urgent. That's not a character flaw. It's a universal pattern, and it's one of the things a good adviser systematically solves.

What accountability actually means

The value of having someone who holds you to your own financial intentions is not about being told what to do. It's about having a structure that makes inaction more difficult than action. A review meeting you can't cancel. A plan that flags when something needs to happen. A person who already knows your full situation and can move quickly when you need them to.

Without that, the best financial intentions in the world tend to remain intentions.

Part four

The honest conversation about cost

There is one part of the kitchen analogy where it breaks down — and it's worth being direct about it.

Some people genuinely cannot afford the premium kitchen. They don't have the budget for the A team. And that's a real constraint, not a failure of will. A 50-grand kitchen fit is not available to everyone, and there's nothing wrong with acknowledging that clearly.

The same is true of premium financial planning. There is a genuine cost to the service — the regulatory requirements alone make it impossible to provide meaningful advice for a nominal fee. That's why there's a minimum. Not as a barrier, but as an honest statement of what the service actually costs to deliver properly.

If the cost of a good financial plan isn't right for your current position, that's a legitimate answer. The answer that isn't legitimate — the one that tends to cost significantly more in the long run — is choosing a cheaper service that can't actually do the job, or concluding you'll manage it yourself and then not managing it at all.

It's not unethical to charge less for a service that provides a load of value. It just feels like poor business sense.
The point about pricing and quality

We are not the cheapest option. We are Chartered Financial Planners, working independently, with the best available planning technology, serving clients who want the A team and are willing to pay for what that actually means. If that's the right fit, the conversation is easy. If it's not, we'll tell you honestly — and point you somewhere more appropriate.

What we won't do is offer a discounted version of the service and call it the same thing. That's the one thing, in the kitchen analogy or anywhere else, that would genuinely not be fair.

Recognise any of this?

Story 03 · Scam prevention
Story 03 · Scam prevention
A glossy brochure.
A guaranteed 12% return.
An NHS pension almost gone.

An anonymous account of how a client came within days of transferring a lifetime’s retirement savings into a scheme that didn’t work the way they were told it did — and what changed when someone with the right knowledge looked at the paperwork.

Client profileProfessional, late 50s
Amount at risk£280,000 in pension savings
How closeTransfer forms already signed
Part one

The phone call

He hadn’t been looking for anything. The call came out of nowhere — friendly, professional, knowledgeable. The person on the line knew what a final salary pension was, knew roughly what his transfer value might be, and had a specific question: had he ever thought about whether he could do better with it?

The answer, of course, was yes. He had thought about it. He was in his late fifties and the number on his pension statement was large — larger than he’d expected. It felt abstract, tied up in something he’d never have to engage with until he retired. The idea that it could be working harder, producing income now, felt like an interesting proposition.

“They sent me a brochure. It looked completely professional. Real photos, real addresses, a legal-sounding structure. I couldn’t find anything wrong with it.”
The client, looking back

The scheme was self-storage units. Industrial properties in the north of England, offering investors a long-term lease on individual units which would then be sublet through a management company. The projected return was quoted at 12% per year. The brochure was glossy. The numbers looked plausible, in the way that numbers designed to look plausible always do.

Part two

What he couldn’t see

This type of scheme has a long and documented history of catastrophic outcomes. By 2017, the Serious Fraud Office had launched a full investigation into self-storage pension investments. By 2025, six individuals had been charged with conspiracy to defraud after almost 2,000 investors transferred a combined £75 million into these products — most of which was unrecoverable. One investor, a former NHS employee, transferred £370,000 out of a “secure and generous” workplace pension and may have lost everything. The Pensions Ombudsman, reviewing his case, described him as “blameless.”

1,900+investors affected
£75mtransferred into the schemes
46%commission paid to promoters

The red flags were there. They are always there, in retrospect. A guaranteed return. A cold call from someone he had never met. A structure involving multiple companies, some offshore. No FCA authorisation for the firm promoting the transfer. A sense of limited-time availability. Every single one of these is a documented warning sign — but they only look like warning signs if you know what you are looking for.

Why these schemes work

Pension scams succeed because they are designed by people who understand exactly how much most savers know about their own pensions — which is very little. The complexity is the cover. A Chartered Financial Planner with a regulated obligation to act in your interests sees through the structure immediately. The average person, handed a glossy brochure with an authoritative-sounding yield, has no framework to question it.

Part three

What the adviser saw

He had just started working with us. It was early in the relationship — the WealthPlan wasn’t yet finished. But he mentioned the opportunity in passing, almost as a footnote: he’d been looking at something that might boost his retirement income. Could we take a look?

We looked.

Within fifteen minutes it was clear. The promoting firm was not on the FCA register. The commission structure — disclosed in the small print — was 46% of the invested amount, paid to a connected company. The “guaranteed return” was not guaranteed in any legal sense. The underlying investment was illiquid by design: once the money was in, it could not come out. The structure was not designed to generate returns for investors. It was designed to extract commissions.

The number that matters

He was about to transfer £280,000 — his entire pension pot, built over thirty years of work — into a scheme that carried a realistic probability of total loss. The transfer forms were already signed. He needed one person to say: stop, look at this, this is not what it appears to be.

That is what we did.

Part four

The value that doesn’t appear in a cashflow model

The value of the intervention is, in one sense, easy to calculate. £280,000 is a number. Losing it is a calculable event. The ongoing income it would have funded — modelled in his WealthPlan at around £14,000 a year in retirement — was gone in the scenario where he made that transfer.

But there is a dimension of this that doesn’t appear in the numbers. Pension scam victims don’t just lose money. They lose the retirement they planned. They frequently lose the confidence to make financial decisions at all. They often experience significant mental health consequences. The Pensions Ombudsman’s case files read not like financial disputes but like personal crises. People who did everything they were supposed to do — worked hard, saved consistently, deferred gratification — and had the result taken from them by someone who knew exactly how to exploit the gap between their trust and their knowledge.

The gap between trust and knowledge is exactly where a good adviser operates. Not to restrict your choices, but to make sure the choices in front of you are what they claim to be.

Part five

What he said afterwards

“I’m an intelligent person. I have a degree. I run a business. And I was days away from making the worst financial decision of my life. Not because I was stupid — because I didn’t have the right knowledge. That’s what you have.”
The client, three months later

That observation matters. Pension scams are not primarily a problem of gullibility. Anyone can be the victim of a pension scam, no matter how financially savvy they think they are, as the FCA puts it. The scams work because they are professionally constructed to look legitimate, and because most people — regardless of their general intelligence or professional success — lack the specific, technical knowledge to identify what is wrong.

A good adviser is not smarter than you. They just know the specific things you do not. And in a world where pension fraud losses totalled £17.5 million in 2024 alone, with an average loss of approximately £34,000 per individual, those are the things that matter most.

Recognise any of this?
Start with a conversation. No commitment required.

If you’ve been approached about a pension opportunity and aren’t sure whether it’s legitimate, we’ll tell you — no charge, no obligation.
