Implementation Guide
What will I need to set up?
Fee calculator guide

What will I need to set up?
A plain-English guide to every implementation option

5 min read — written to help you fill in the fee calculator accurately

Most people sit down with the fee calculator and hit a wall at Section 4 — "what do you need us to set up?" This guide walks through every option in plain English: what it is, who typically needs it, and how to know whether it applies to you.

You don't need to know exactly what you need — that's partly what the planning process is for. If you're genuinely unsure about something, tick it anyway and we'll work it out together in your first conversation. Also worth knowing: we automatically identify your main piece of work (the most complex item) and list everything else as additional. Adding more items doesn't always raise the fee proportionally — the tier cap and complexity discount apply to the total.

Investments & ISAs

Straightforward

Opening a new ISA

A tax-free wrapper for your savings or investments. Any growth, dividends, or interest inside it is completely free of tax, forever. You can put in up to £20,000 per tax year per person.

Tick this if
You have cash or investments you'd like to shelter from tax
You haven't used your ISA allowance this year
You and a partner both want one — set the count to 2
Skip this if
You already have an ISA and just want it managed — include it in Section 5 instead
You're only transferring — use the transfer option below
Straightforward

Opening a general investment account (GIA)

A flexible investment account with no annual limit and no restrictions on withdrawals. It's taxable — but there's an annual capital gains allowance, and we'll structure withdrawals to use it as efficiently as possible.

Tick this if
You've used your ISA allowance and have more to invest
You're investing a large lump sum and need to drip-feed into ISAs over time
Skip this if
You haven't maxed your ISA yet — put money there first, it's more tax-efficient
Straightforward

Junior ISA or Junior pension (for a child or grandchild)

A Junior ISA lets a child access money at 18. A Junior pension (Junior SIPP) locks money away until age 57 — but you get 20% tax relief on contributions right now, making it a powerful long-term gift.

Tick this if
You want to put money away for a child or grandchild
You'd like to help a child start building long-term wealth early
Set the count to the number of children
Skip this if
The child already has an account — include it in Section 5 instead
Straightforward

Setting up an investment bond

An insurance-based investment wrapper — not a savings bond. It lets you take up to 5% of your original investment each year as income without an immediate tax charge, making it useful for tax-efficient regular withdrawals and estate planning.

Tick this if
You want to take a regular income in a tax-efficient way
Inheritance tax planning is part of what you want to address
You're a higher-rate taxpayer with a large lump sum to invest
Skip this if
You're a basic-rate taxpayer — an ISA or GIA will usually be simpler and just as effective
Straightforward

New ISA / New ISA with transfer(s) in

A tax-free wrapper for your savings or investments. Any growth, dividends, or interest inside it is completely free of tax, forever. You can put in up to £20,000 per tax year per person.

If you have existing ISAs or investments sitting elsewhere, we can open the new ISA and transfer them in as part of the same piece of work. Select New ISA with transfer(s) in and use the How many transfers in? counter to tell us how many separate policies you want to consolidate — each one involves its own research and admin. The cost is slightly higher than a plain new ISA to reflect that extra work, but it's still all one report.

New ISA — tick if
You want to open a fresh ISA with new money only
You and a partner both want one — set the account count to 2
New ISA with transfer(s) in — tick if
You want a new ISA and want to bring one or more existing policies across at the same time
Use the transfers-in counter to set how many policies you're transferring
Straightforward

New GIA / New GIA with transfer(s) in

A flexible investment account with no annual limit and no restrictions on withdrawals. It's taxable — but there's an annual capital gains allowance, and we'll structure withdrawals to use it efficiently. Same transfer(s) in logic as the ISA above applies — use the transfers-in counter to set how many policies you're consolidating.

New GIA — tick if
You've used your ISA allowance and have more to invest with new money
New GIA with transfer(s) in — tick if
You want a new GIA and want to consolidate one or more existing investment accounts at the same time
Skip this if
You haven't maxed your ISA yet — put money there first, it's more tax-efficient
Straightforward

Junior ISA or Junior pension / with transfer(s) in

A Junior ISA lets a child access money at 18. A Junior pension (Junior SIPP) locks money away until age 57 — but you get 20% tax relief on contributions right now. Same transfer-in logic applies if there's an existing junior account to consolidate.

Tick this if
You want to put money away for a child or grandchild
Set the count to the number of children
Skip this if
The child already has an account and you just want it managed ongoing — include it in Section 5
Straightforward

Transfer into an existing account (non-pension)

If you already have an ISA, GIA, or other investment account set up with us — or one is being set up as a separate item in this work — and you want to transfer another existing policy into it, this is the option to use. There's no new account being opened here; it's purely the research and admin involved in transferring an existing policy in.

Tick this if
You have an existing account (already set up or being set up) and want to consolidate additional old policies into it
Set the count to the number of separate transfers — each one is priced separately as the research and admin applies per policy
Don't use this if
You're opening a new account and transferring in at the same time — use the relevant "with transfer(s) in" option above instead
Straightforward

Investment bond

An insurance-based investment wrapper — not a savings bond. It lets you take up to 5% of your original investment each year as income without an immediate tax charge, making it useful for tax-efficient regular withdrawals and estate planning. Slightly more involved than a straightforward ISA or GIA given the additional technical work required.

Tick this if
You want to take a regular income in a tax-efficient way
Inheritance tax planning is part of what you want to address
You're a higher-rate taxpayer with a large lump sum to invest
Skip this if
You're a basic-rate taxpayer — an ISA or GIA will usually be simpler and just as effective
Straightforward

Fund switch within an existing account

If you have an existing investment account, ISA, or pension that's already on a platform but invested in the wrong funds — perhaps a legacy default fund or something no longer aligned to your goals — we can switch it into the right strategy. This doesn't involve opening a new account or transferring to a new provider.

Tick this if
You have an existing account that needs reinvesting into a different strategy
You want to move out of a default fund you were auto-enrolled into
Skip this if
You need to move to a different platform entirely — that's a transfer, use the option above

Pensions

Straightforward

New personal pension (SIPP) / New SIPP with transfer(s) in

A self-invested personal pension you control. The government adds 20% tax relief on contributions — higher-rate taxpayers can claim back more through their tax return. Contributions can come from you personally or your company.

If you also want to bring existing pensions across into the new SIPP, select New SIPP with transfer(s) in and use the How many transfers in? counter to tell us how many pension schemes you want to consolidate. Pension transfers involve more work than investment transfers — there's a statutory process, additional regulatory requirements, and careful suitability analysis per scheme — which is reflected in the higher cost compared to a new SIPP alone.

New SIPP — tick if
You want to open a new pension with new contributions only
You're self-employed and don't have a workplace pension
New SIPP with transfer(s) in — tick if
You want a new pension and want to transfer one or more existing pensions into it at the same time
Use the transfers-in counter to tell us how many pension schemes you're consolidating
Moderate

Transfer into an existing pension

If you already have a pension set up with us — or one is being set up as a separate item in this work — and you want to transfer additional old pensions into it, this covers the research and admin for each additional transfer. There's no new pension being opened; it's the transfer work only.

Tick this if
You have multiple old pensions to consolidate into an existing or newly set-up pension
Set the count to the number of additional pension transfers
Don't use this if
You're opening a new pension and transferring in at the same time — use "New SIPP with transfer(s) in" above
Your pension has guaranteed benefits (final salary) — use the option below
Complex

Transferring a pension with a guarantee (final salary / defined benefit)

Final salary pensions promise a guaranteed income in retirement — usually a proportion of your salary, for life. Transferring means giving up that guarantee in exchange for a lump sum. This is one of the most significant financial decisions a person can make, and we treat it with appropriate care. We won't recommend a transfer unless it's clearly in your interest.

This applies if
You have a final salary pension from a previous employer
You've received a transfer value (CETV) and want to explore whether it makes sense
Probably doesn't apply if
Your pension is from a modern workplace scheme without a guaranteed income promise
Moderate

Taking your first tax free cash payment from your pension

When you first access your pension, you're typically entitled to take up to 25% of the fund as a tax-free lump sum. This is a one-off event and one of the most important decisions in the run-up to retirement — getting the timing and structure right can make a significant difference to your lifetime tax position. We'll model this carefully using your cashflow plan before making any recommendation.

Tick this if
You've reached pension access age (currently 55, rising to 57 in 2028) and want to take your tax-free cash
You're planning to crystallise your pension benefits for the first time
You want to move into drawdown alongside taking your tax-free cash
Skip this if
You've already crystallised your pension and taken your tax-free cash previously
You're many years from retirement and just want to grow your pension
Moderate

Buying an annuity

An annuity converts your pension pot into a guaranteed income — typically for life. You give up flexibility in exchange for certainty. Annuity rates vary significantly between providers, and the difference between a good and average rate can be worth tens of thousands of pounds over a lifetime.

Tick this if
You want certainty over income in retirement above everything else
You're in poor health — you may qualify for an enhanced annuity rate
Skip this if
You want flexibility to take more or less in different years
You have significant guaranteed income already (state pension, final salary)

Protection

Moderate

Personal life cover or income protection

If you died or couldn't work due to illness or injury, would your family be financially secure? This includes life insurance, critical illness cover, and income protection — arranged in your own name.

A note on how we charge for protection: Life cover and income protection are the one area where we receive commission from the insurer rather than charging you a fee. We do this because we want everyone to have appropriate cover — and a fixed advice fee can make smaller policies feel prohibitively expensive, which means people go without. We recognise this creates a conflict of interest. Read how we manage it →
Tick this if
You have dependants who rely on your income
You have a mortgage that couldn't be paid without your income
You're self-employed with no employer sick pay
You haven't reviewed your cover in the last 3 years
Skip this if
You've recently reviewed and are confident your cover is adequate
Moderate

Business protection

If a key director or shareholder died or became seriously ill, what would happen to the business? Business protection covers key person insurance, shareholder protection, and relevant life cover — a tax-efficient way for a company to provide death benefits for a director.

Tick this if
You're a business owner or company director
Your business would be at risk if you or a co-director couldn't work
You have a business partner with no shareholder protection agreement
Skip this if
You're employed rather than a director or owner — personal protection is more relevant

Specialist

Complex

SSAS (small self-administered pension scheme)

A bespoke occupational pension for company directors. Unlike a standard SIPP, a SSAS can lend money back to the sponsoring company, purchase commercial property (including your own business premises), and is more flexible in how it's invested. It comes with significant complexity and ongoing obligations.

Relevant if
You're a director who wants to hold commercial property inside a pension
You want to lend money from your pension to your business
Probably not relevant if
You want a straightforward personal pension — a SIPP will do the job more simply
Complex

VCT (Venture Capital Trust)

A VCT is a listed company that invests in smaller, early-stage UK businesses. Investing in a VCT offers up to 30% income tax relief on the amount invested, tax-free dividends, and no capital gains tax on disposal — in exchange for taking on higher investment risk and committing for at least five years.

Relevant if
You have a significant income tax bill you'd like to reduce
You're comfortable with higher risk and a five-year minimum hold
You've already maximised pension and ISA allowances
Not relevant if
You want stable, accessible investments
You may need the money within five years
Complex

EIS (Enterprise Investment Scheme)

EIS allows you to invest directly in qualifying smaller UK companies and claim up to 30% income tax relief, plus defer capital gains tax and eliminate inheritance tax after a two-year hold. The risk is higher than mainstream investments — you're investing in early-stage businesses — but the tax advantages can be significant for the right client.

Relevant if
You have a large income tax or CGT liability to manage
Inheritance tax planning is a priority
You're a higher or additional rate taxpayer comfortable with illiquid investments
Not relevant if
You want low-risk or easily accessible investments
You might need the capital within three years
Complex

Business Relief investment

Business Relief (BR) investments qualify for 100% inheritance tax relief after a two-year hold, making them a powerful IHT planning tool — particularly for clients who want to retain access to their capital (unlike a gift or trust). They invest in unlisted or AIM-listed businesses and carry more risk than mainstream investments.

Relevant if
Inheritance tax mitigation is a priority and you want to keep access to the money
You've considered or exhausted other IHT options (gifts, trusts, pension)
You're comfortable with the underlying investment risk
Not relevant if
You want low-risk capital preservation
You don't have a meaningful IHT exposure

If you're still unsure after reading this, tick what seems relevant and we'll refine it in your first conversation. Nothing is binding at this stage — the calculator is just to give us both a realistic starting point.

Why we built this

A little while ago, a business owner got in touch with us. She was approaching a significant exit and needed a financial planner she could trust. We had a good conversation. We genuinely liked her and she said how much she'd enjoyed the meeting. And then she chose someone else.

But she took the time to tell us why — and it was one of the most useful pieces of feedback we've ever received.

She said our fixed fee model was hard to compare. The other firm she was considering charged a percentage of her money — so if she had £5m to invest, she could do the maths herself in seconds. With us, she had no idea what she'd be paying until we'd actually sat down and worked through her situation together. It felt like a leap of faith she wasn't willing to take before she'd even decided whether we were the right fit.

She was right. And she didn't have to tell us — but she did.

So we built this. A straightforward way to work out what you'd pay — before you've spoken to anyone, without any obligation, and in enough detail that you can use it to compare us against any other firm you're considering. That's what this page is for.

How our fees are structured

We charge in two ways: an upfront fee for the work we do to get you set up, and an ongoing annual fee for the advice and service we provide year after year.

What we don't charge for is worth knowing too. We don't charge for investment management, fund switches, top-ups to existing plans, or regular withdrawals. Many advice firms charge for all of these.

Section 2 — WealthPlan
Are you starting with a WealthPlan?
WealthPlan is our financial planning process — the starting point for most new client relationships. It's a structured, collaborative exercise that builds a clear picture of where you are now, where you want to get to, and exactly how your money will get you there. It costs £2,495 and typically takes 6–8 weeks from first meeting to written strategy.

Think of WealthPlan like a thorough health check combined with a roadmap. Before we make a single recommendation, we need to understand the full picture — your financial life today, the goals and the worries, what you've got, what you owe, and what you actually want your money to do for you.

Step 1 — Initial meeting

We get to know each other. You tell us what's brought you here and what you're hoping to achieve. No paperwork, no forms — just a conversation. This is where we decide whether we're a good fit for each other.

Step 2 — Discovery meeting

A deeper conversation about your goals, your priorities, and what financial freedom actually looks like for you. We'll challenge you (gently), gather the facts we need, and start to map out the opportunities and risks in your current situation.

Step 3 — Building your financial strategy

We build a detailed model of your financial future using Voyant — the leading cashflow planning tool used by the UK's top financial planners. We test different scenarios: what if you retire at 55? What if markets fall? What if you stop working for two years? You see the numbers before you make any decisions.

Step 4 — Your written WealthPlan

We produce a clear, written financial plan that includes your family balance sheet, cashflow projections, scenario modelling, tax planning opportunities, and a prioritised action list. Not a brochure — a real working document that guides every decision we make together going forward.

What's included in the annual ongoing fee after WealthPlan is complete: Once your WealthPlan exists, keeping it current is part of your ongoing annual service — at no extra charge. That means annual reviews of your cashflow model, updated projections as your life changes, regular tax planning, and ongoing refinement of the strategy. The plan doesn't sit in a drawer — it's a living document we work from throughout the relationship.
Starting WealthPlan? Begin with the Grab Life Wheel. Before we talk about your finances, we need to understand your life — what matters, what energises you, and where you feel most fulfilled. IHT @ 40% (or 36% )
Why 36%?

HMRC allows a reduced IHT rate of 36% (instead of 40%) when at least 10% of the "net estate" is left to registered charities.

The "net estate" is your estate value after deducting the nil-rate band, residence nil-rate band, and other reliefs — but before the charitable deduction itself.

In some cases, leaving a relatively small extra amount to charity can actually increase what your beneficiaries receive, because the tax saving on the remaining estate outweighs the additional charitable gift.

Important caveats & assumptions
  • This calculator is a guide only and does not constitute financial, legal or tax advice. It is based on current (2024/25) HMRC rules and the proposed April 2027 pension changes, which may change before implementation.
  • Nil-rate band assumed at £325,000 per person. Residence nil-rate band assumed at £175,000 per person. Both are frozen until at least April 2030.
  • The RNRB is tapered by £1 for every £2 the net estate exceeds £2,000,000. This taper applies both before and after the pension changes, and the pension inclusion may push you into (or further into) the taper zone.
  • Business relief (BR) at 100% applies to interests in qualifying unincorporated businesses, unquoted company shares, and AIM shares held for 2+ years. 50% relief applies to controlling interests in quoted companies and certain business assets. BR rules are complex — take professional advice. From April 2026, BR will be capped at £1m for 100% relief and 50% relief thereafter.
  • The pension changes (Finance Bill 2024) will bring most uncrystallised defined contribution pension funds into the IHT estate from April 2027. Defined benefit pensions, pensions already in drawdown, and death-in-service payments are treated differently. These rules had not been finalised at the time this tool was built.
  • Gifts made within 7 years of death may be subject to IHT under the 7-year rule, with taper relief on gifts made 3–7 years before death. The annual gift exemption (£3,000/yr) is excluded from this calculation.
  • The charitable giving rate reduction (36% instead of 40%) applies only where the charitable bequest equals or exceeds 10% of the net estate after nil-rate bands and other deductions.
  • This tool does not model: agricultural property relief, woodlands relief, heritage assets, complex trust structures, deeds of variation, or any interaction with income tax on pension withdrawals.
  • Xentum Financial Planning Ltd is authorised and regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority. Estate planning involves complex tax rules — always obtain a written report from a qualified financial planner before making decisions.

Your details
Your name

Date of disposal / tax year
For shares in a personal company, all three conditions below must be met for at least two years before disposal. Tick Yes to each that applies to you.
BADR qualifying conditions
All three required — for at least 2 years prior to disposal
You own at least 5% of the ordinary share capital
You must hold at least 5% of the company's ordinary shares and have done so for the 2-year qualifying period. Anti-dilution provisions under S.169S TCGA 1992 may help if your stake was diluted by new share issues — worth checking with your adviser.
You are (or were) an officer or employee of the company
You must be a director, company secretary, or employee. A shareholder who is not an officer or employee does not qualify — this is the most commonly missed condition. The role must have been held throughout the 2-year period.
The company is a trading company (or holding company of a trading group)
HMRC requires the company's activities to be "wholly or mainly" trading. Investment activities — holding significant cash, property portfolios, or investment assets — can jeopardise this. The 80/20 rule is a useful guide but not a legal test. BADR does not apply to investment companies.
You have 5%+ of voting rights and entitlement to 5%+ of profits & winding-up proceeds
From April 2019, you must also be entitled to at least 5% of the company's distributable profits and net assets on a winding up — not just share capital. Alphabet share structures with restricted rights on dividends can fail this test.
BADR does not apply to: Investment companies, property investment businesses (unless incidental), furnished holiday lettings (from April 2025), or gains deferred through EIS relief being triggered. Cessation of trade — if the company has stopped trading — must be within 3 years of disposal for BADR to apply.
Total sale proceeds
The amount you receive for your shares — cash, deferred consideration, and loan notes at face value
£
Total base cost (book cost)
What you paid for the shares — see the guide below for what qualifies
£
Allowable costs & expenses
Professional fees directly related to the disposal — legal, accountancy, valuation (not advisory fees)
£
Enhancement expenditure
Capital expenditure that enhanced the value of your shares (rare for shares — more relevant for property)
£
What your base cost almost certainly includes
  • The subscription price you paid for your shares — typically the nominal value when you incorporated (often just £1 per share). For many founders who set up a company with 100 shares at £1, the base cost is just £100.
  • Any further consideration paid for additional shares — if you subscribed for further shares in a funding round, the amount you paid is added to your base cost.
  • Amounts treated as consideration under S.17 TCGA — for example, if shares were acquired in exchange for assets transferred at market value.
What does NOT increase your base cost in a private company
  • Retained profits left in the company — the single biggest misconception. Cash you earned and left in the business does not increase what you "paid" for the shares. It belongs to the company, not to your personal cost base.
  • Time and effort invested in building the business — sweat equity has no CGT base cost. Your contribution of skill and time is not recognised as a cost for CGT purposes.
  • Director's loans or salary not drawn — leaving remuneration in the company increases the company's assets, but does not increase your personal share cost. However, if you have an outstanding director's loan account, that is a separate debt owed to you and sits outside the share gain entirely.
  • Goodwill built up over time — the increasing value of the business (goodwill, IP, customer contracts) is the gain, not a cost.
This is why a founder who incorporates a company for £100 and sells for £5,000,000 has a gain of £4,999,900 — not a smaller figure. The entire increase in value above what you paid for the shares is taxable.
What CAN legitimately reduce your taxable gain
  • BADR itself — reduces the tax rate on the first £1m of qualifying gains from 24% to 18% (saving up to £60,000 from 6 April 2026).
  • Annual CGT exempt amount — £3,000 for 2026/27 (this calculator includes it automatically).
  • Genuine allowable costs — legal and accountancy fees for the sale, valuation fees, HMRC-recognised advisory costs directly related to the disposal.
  • Capital losses — losses from other CGT disposals in the same or earlier tax years can be offset against your gain.
  • EIS / SEIS reinvestment relief — if you reinvest into qualifying companies, you can defer or exempt part of the gain. This requires careful planning ahead of the sale.
  • Earn-outs and deferred consideration — if part of the proceeds are contingent on future performance, those amounts are assessed to CGT in the year they crystallise, not the year of the main sale.
If you have a director's loan account outstanding at completion, you should receive repayment of that separately. This is NOT a capital gain — it's a repayment of a debt. Make sure your solicitors and accountant structure this correctly in the sale agreement.
Employee Ownership Trusts (EOT)
  • If you are selling to an Employee Ownership Trust and meet the qualifying conditions, the entire gain may be exempt from CGT — not just taxed at 10%. This is a significant planning opportunity that should be explored before deciding on a buyer structure.
Get professional advice. The rules around base cost, allowable deductions, and BADR eligibility are complex. A mistake — particularly on the two-year qualifying period, the trading company test, or the structuring of earn-outs — can be extremely costly. Always work with a qualified accountant and tax adviser before completing any sale.

Important caveats & assumptions
  • This calculator uses 2026/27 CGT rates: BADR 18% (from 6 April 2026), standard rate 24% (higher rate taxpayer), 18% (basic rate). The BADR rate increased from 10% (2024/25) to 14% (2025/26) to 18% (2026/27 onwards). These rates apply to non-residential assets including shares.
  • The BADR lifetime limit is £1,000,000. Any gain above this limit (or where the limit is already exhausted) is taxed at the standard CGT rate. The lifetime limit is cumulative across all qualifying disposals in all tax years.
  • The CGT annual exempt amount is £3,000 for 2026/27. This calculator assumes it has not been used on other gains — adjust "Other capital gains this year" if it has been partially used.
  • The basic/higher rate boundary determines whether any non-BADR gain falls at 18% or 24%. If your income uses up the basic rate band (£50,270 for 2026/27), all non-BADR gains are at 24%.
  • Earn-out provisions: if your sale includes deferred consideration contingent on performance, the tax on those amounts will be assessed in the year they are received, not the year of the main disposal. BADR may still apply to the deferred amounts if the original disposal qualified.
  • This calculator does not model: Investors' Relief (10% rate on external investor gains, separate £10m lifetime limit), EIS/SEIS CGT deferral, holdover relief, rollover relief, employee ownership trust exemptions, or non-resident CGT rules.
  • This is a guide only and does not constitute financial or tax advice. Capital gains tax legislation is complex and subject to change. Always work with a qualified accountant before completing a disposal.

Important caveats & notes
  • This checklist is a guide only and does not constitute financial, legal or tax advice. EOT eligibility involves complex legislation (Schedule 37, Finance Act 2014 and subsequent amendments) and must be confirmed by qualified legal and tax advisers.
  • The CGT exemption on an EOT sale applies to all selling shareholders, regardless of size of stake — there is no minimum holding period. However, all sellers must be disposing at the same time as part of the same EOT acquisition.
  • The £3,600 income-tax-free bonus limit applies per eligible employee per tax year. Bonuses must be paid on equal terms (though they can vary by hours worked, salary, length of service, or combination). NI contributions are still due on bonuses above £3,600 is incorrect — NI is due on all amounts; only income tax is exempt up to £3,600.
  • The connected persons rule (≤40% of employees post-sale) applies to former owners and their connected persons (spouses, civil partners, children, parents, siblings, and companies under their control). Former owners who remain as employees count towards this 40%.
  • From October 2024, new rules require the EOT trustees to be independent of the selling shareholders, and a new clawback mechanism applies if conditions are breached within 4 years. These changes apply to disposals from 30 October 2024 onwards.
  • The majority ownership test requires the EOT to acquire and retain more than 50% of ordinary shares. The EOT can acquire in stages as long as it holds majority at completion.
  • This tool uses 2026/27 tax rules. BADR and CGT rates referenced: standard 24%/18%; BADR 18% from 6 April 2026. EOT CGT exemption rates unchanged.

Xentum Corporate · EOT Insight
Three things nobody tells you about selling to an Employee Ownership Trust
From the Pro Manchester EOT Summit, May 2025
Ed Stubbs
Chartered Financial Planner, Xentum Corporate
May 2025
5 min read

Last month I was at the Pro Manchester EOT Summit — a room full of M&A advisers, tax specialists, and business owners all working through the same question: is an Employee Ownership Trust the right exit for me? Three speakers said something that cut through the noise. I wrote them down because they're exactly what I wish more business owners heard before they signed anything.

The EOT route has become increasingly popular since its introduction in 2014 — and rightly so. Zero CGT for selling shareholders. Income-tax-free bonuses of up to £3,600 per employee per year. A structure that keeps the business in the hands of the people who built it. On paper, it looks almost too good to be true.

The reality, as with most things in exit planning, is more nuanced. The financial mechanics are well-documented. What isn't talked about as openly is everything else — the culture, the psychology, the structuring decisions that determine whether an EOT sale actually works. That's what the three speakers below each addressed in their own way.

The three things they said

Insight 1 of 3
If your culture isn't right before going employee owned via an employee ownership trust, selling to an EOT won't solve it.
RG
Richard Gahagan
Founder, We Are Adam

This is the one that makes business owners uncomfortable, because it implies that the EOT is not a solution to a problem — it's an amplifier of whatever already exists. A company with strong employee engagement, clear communication, and a genuine sense of shared purpose will thrive under employee ownership. The opposite is also true.

The structure transfers ownership, not culture. If people don't already feel invested in the business — if the management team isn't ready to lead without the founder's shadow, if transparency around financials is absent, if there's no meaningful way for employees to influence decisions — then the EOT will surface those gaps, not paper over them.

The practical implication for business owners is this: if you're thinking about an EOT sale in the next three to five years, the work you need to do now isn't just financial. It's building the infrastructure of an employee-owned business before you need it. Shared P&L awareness. Regular business updates. A management team that runs the business, not just executes orders. A clear answer to the question employees will ask on day one: what does this actually mean for me?

From a financial planning perspective, this also matters because the value of the business is tied to its sustainability post-sale. An EOT that struggles because the culture wasn't ready will repay the founders more slowly — and potentially not at all.

This hit hardest in the room. Several founders shifted in their seats. The EOT is often pitched as the exit that lets you do good — for your employees, your legacy, the community. And it can be. But it has to be built on something real. The business has to be genuinely ready for a different kind of ownership, which means the people in it have to be ready too.

Insight 2 of 3
Don't sell to an employee ownership trust for tax purposes only — do it for the long-term benefit of all involved.
HH
Hasan Hashmi
Tax Adviser, MHA

Coming from a tax adviser, this is a striking thing to say. Hasan has worked on dozens of EOT transactions. His point was not that the tax benefit is unimportant — zero CGT on a £5m sale is transformative — but that it cannot be the only reason to go down this route.

The concern is structural. HMRC and the courts have become increasingly attentive to EOT arrangements that look like tax avoidance with governance theatre bolted on. The October 2024 changes — including the requirement for independent trustees and a new clawback mechanism — were specifically designed to address EOTs where the founders retained effective control while claiming the CGT exemption.

An EOT driven purely by tax motivations is also more likely to struggle commercially. The founders may not be genuinely invested in making it work for employees. The employees may not feel any real change. The trustee arrangements may be minimal. Three years in, the structure starts to look fragile — and HMRC is paying closer attention than it was.

The EOT exemption is extraordinarily generous. It is one of the best tax reliefs available to a UK business owner. But it works best — and is most durable — when it reflects a genuine commitment to the principles behind it: that employees should share in the value they've helped create. If that's not genuinely your position, there are other exit routes worth exploring.

The 2026/27 EOT landscape

The EOT CGT exemption remains unchanged in the 2026/27 tax year — no CGT on qualifying disposals, £3,600 income-tax-free annual bonuses per eligible employee. However, the October 2024 rules (requiring at least one independent trustee and introducing a 4-year clawback on breach of conditions) have raised the bar for what a properly structured EOT looks like. This is the environment Hasan was referring to — and it makes the "do it properly or don't do it" argument more important than ever.

Insight 3 of 3
Consider the option of using debt to finance more upfront consideration for the founders if the business can cope with the ongoing interest payments.
JC
Jeremy Cole
M&A Broker, Cole Associates

This is the one that most founders haven't thought about — and it's the one where financial planning adds direct value. The typical EOT structure involves the trust paying the founders over time out of the business's future profits. This is fine, but it means the founders are essentially providing deferred consideration — carrying the risk that the business continues to perform — while waiting years for the full sale proceeds.

External debt financing changes that equation. If the business takes on a loan — from a bank, a private lender, or through an asset-backed structure — the EOT can pay a larger proportion of the consideration upfront. The business then services the debt from future profits rather than the founders waiting for distributions.

The key question is whether the business can comfortably service the debt. A business generating £500k of EBITDA with clean balance sheet, recurring revenues, and a strong management team is a very different proposition to one with lumpy revenues and thin margins. Jeremy's point is that the option is often not even discussed — advisers default to the deferred consideration model without testing whether debt might serve the founders better.

For founders who need liquidity — to fund retirement, reinvest in other ventures, or simply because they've waited long enough — the ability to receive more cash at completion is significant. The tax treatment of both structures should be reviewed carefully, and the business's ability to service debt is not guaranteed. But it's a conversation that should be had.

Jeremy's point lands particularly well for business owners who have been told the EOT is inherently a "patient" exit — that they just have to accept receiving consideration over five to seven years. That's not always true. The right capital structure can materially change the personal financial outcome for the founders, and it's worth exploring before heads of terms are agreed.

What this means if you're considering an EOT

These three insights don't argue against the EOT — quite the opposite. They argue for doing it properly, for the right reasons, with the right structure. An EOT that ticks all three boxes — genuine culture readiness, authentic intent to benefit employees, and an optimised financing structure — is one of the best exits available to a UK business owner today.

The financial case is compelling. Zero CGT. £3,600 per employee per year in income-tax-free bonuses. A business that stays independent. A legacy the founder can be proud of. But the path to that outcome requires planning — usually starting two to three years before a sale is on the table.

A note on timing

The most common mistake I see with EOT planning is leaving it too late. By the time a strategic buyer is on the scene or a heads of terms has been drafted, the window for meaningful EOT structuring has often closed. The trustee arrangements, the employee communication plan, the debt financing analysis — these all take time. If you're three to five years from a potential exit, now is exactly the right time to start the conversation.

The EOT Eligibility Checker above is a starting point — it will tell you whether the basic conditions are met. But eligibility is just the threshold. What makes the difference is the quality of the planning that follows.

Ready to explore the EOT route properly?

I work exclusively with business owners planning for exit. If you're thinking about an EOT sale — now or in the next few years — the earlier we talk, the more options you have.

Most people never get round to it. A will sits at the bottom of the to-do list for years — it's not urgent, it's not fun, and nothing bad happens immediately if you skip it. The fact that you have one puts you ahead of the majority. This tool won't second-guess what's in it — but it will show you how your assets flow, and flag anything worth a conversation.

Has anything on this list happened since you last wrote or reviewed your will?
Any of these can make a will outdated or legally ineffective — even if the will itself is perfectly written.
Your will may need updating

One or more of the events above typically means a will no longer reflects your intentions — or is partially or fully revoked by law. A solicitor can advise on what needs changing; we can help you think through the financial and estate planning implications.

And when was your will last reviewed?
Even without major life events, tax legislation changes. The nil-rate band, residence nil-rate band, and IHT rules on pensions and business assets have all shifted in recent years.
Worth a review regardless of life events. Even a well-drafted will can become tax-inefficient if legislation changes around it. The nil-rate band freeze, the April 2027 pension IHT changes, and recent updates to business relief all affect how efficiently wealth passes to the next generation. A review every 3–5 years is good practice.
Who does your will leave your estate to?
Enter your main beneficiaries — this powers the inheritance flow diagram below.
⚠ No will — the law decides, not you

A will is one of those things that sits at the very bottom of most people's to-do lists. It feels morbid, it's easy to put off, and nothing bad happens immediately if you don't do it. Until it does. Without a will, your estate passes under the Rules of Intestacy (England & Wales). These rules are fixed by statute — they cannot account for your relationships, wishes, or circumstances. The results can be dramatically different from what you'd actually want.

Key things the intestacy rules do not do:

  • They do not recognise unmarried partners — regardless of how long you have been together, a cohabiting partner receives nothing.
  • They do not recognise step-children unless formally adopted.
  • They do not allow for unequal distribution between children, even if that is what you would want.
  • They do not allow you to exclude someone you have fallen out with.
  • They do not name guardians for your children — a court decides.

Pensions

What we mean by a pension here

Defined contribution (DC) pensions are pensions where money has been paid in — by you, your employer, or both — and the fund has grown over time. This includes SIPPs, workplace DC pensions, and personal pensions. There is a specific pot of money with a value.

Here is the critical thing: your pension sits completely outside your will. It is not part of your estate. It does not pass to whoever your will says. It is governed entirely by the scheme rules — and, more practically, by whether you have completed a nomination of beneficiaries form (also called an expression of wishes).

Without a completed, up-to-date nomination, the trustees decide. They will look for financial dependants. They will usually find a spouse. But in blended families, second marriages, estranged relationships, or simply where life has moved on — there is no guarantee.

A story worth knowing
"A client of mine realised — during a review meeting, with his current wife sitting right next to him — that his ex-wife was still named as the beneficiary on one of his old pensions. He went bright red. His wife glared at him across the table. We updated the nomination that afternoon."
— Ed Stubbs, Xentum
Story shared anonymously.
Common reasons nominations go wrong
→Never completed one. Many people simply don't know the form exists, or assume the pension will follow their will. It won't.
→Not updated after major life events. Divorce, remarriage, death of a named beneficiary, estrangement — none of these automatically update your nomination.
→Named the estate rather than individuals. This pulls the pension into your estate, potentially triggering IHT, defeating the purpose of the pension being outside the estate in the first place.
→Multiple pensions, only one updated. People often have several pensions from different employers and providers. They update the one they think about and forget the others.

Xentum Family · Estate Planning

My Estate —
the booklet every executor will thank you for

Everything your executors, beneficiaries and loved ones will need when the time comes — gathered in one place, completed with your adviser, kept updated.

8 min read Estate Planning Xentum Family

Benjamin Franklin’s observation that death and taxes are life’s only certainties is over two centuries old. The taxes part is something we work on together continuously. The other certainty is one we help you prepare for — not with morbidity, but with care and clarity.

The My Estate booklet exists because the practical aftermath of a death is surprisingly difficult to navigate. Executors face an immediate administrative mountain: locating a will, identifying assets, notifying institutions, dealing with outstanding debts, applying for probate. When the information is scattered — or simply doesn’t exist — that mountain becomes much harder to climb. When it’s gathered in one document, kept updated, and known about in advance, it is manageable.

“The greatest gift you can give your executor isn’t money. It’s a document that tells them exactly where everything is.”

What the booklet covers

The My Estate booklet walks through every area an executor will need to address, in a logical order. It’s designed to be completed gradually — with your adviser, at your own pace — and revisited whenever your circumstances change.

Your will and key legal documents

Where the original will is held, when it was made, who drew it up, and whether a letter of wishes exists. These are the first questions an executor will ask. Having the answers written down saves significant time and prevents the worst-case scenario: a will that cannot be located.

Executors and beneficiaries

The names, addresses and contact details of your executors and the people who will benefit from your estate. Executors need to know they have been appointed; beneficiaries need to be reachable. Neither should have to rely on family memory to find this information.

Powers of attorney

Whether a Lasting Power of Attorney is in place, what type it covers (property and financial affairs, or health and welfare), whether it is registered with the Office of the Public Guardian, and who the named attorneys are. If you lose capacity before death — through illness, dementia, or accident — a registered LPA is the document that allows your affairs to continue to be managed. Without it, an application to the Court of Protection may be required, which is slow and expensive.

1 in 3
People in the UK die without a valid will
6–12
Months a typical probate takes to complete
40%
IHT rate on estates above the nil-rate threshold

Nil-rate band and previous spouse

If you were previously married or in a civil partnership, and your spouse died without using their full inheritance tax nil-rate band, that unused portion can be transferred to your estate — potentially saving tens of thousands of pounds. This requires specific documents: a copy of the grant of representation, the will, the death certificate and the marriage certificate. The booklet prompts you to note where these are held.

Gifts and potentially exempt transfers

Gifts made within seven years of death can affect your IHT position under the ‘seven-year rule’. The booklet provides a record of significant gifts — date, amount, recipient — so your executor has what they need to complete the inheritance tax return accurately. Without this record, the calculation is a guess.

Financial accounts

Bank accounts, building societies, credit cards, loans, ISAs, online accounts — each with sort codes, account numbers and contact details. This is the list your executor will work through to gather the assets of the estate. Incomplete information here means delay. Complete information means the process moves efficiently.

Miscellaneous and digital accounts

Utility companies, insurance policies, club memberships, charities. And increasingly important: digital accounts — email, cloud storage, financial platforms, subscription services. The booklet recommends that passwords and access details for online accounts are recorded somewhere safe and accessible to your executor, distinct from the booklet itself.

“An executor who can’t access a digital account may face months of correspondence with platforms that have no clear bereavement process. A note of login details removes this problem entirely.”

The duties of an executor

Being named as someone’s executor is an honour, but it carries real responsibilities. The main tasks are to identify and value all assets at the date of death; to identify and pay all outstanding debts; and to distribute the net estate in accordance with the will. These steps require applying for a grant of probate (or confirmation in Scotland), completing inheritance tax returns, and dealing with any claims against the estate.

The practical workload depends heavily on how organised the deceased’s affairs were. An executor working from a complete, up-to-date My Estate booklet faces a manageable administrative task. An executor starting from scratch — tracking down accounts, locating insurance policies, working out what’s owed — faces something considerably harder.

Keeping it updated

The booklet is not a one-time exercise. Circumstances change: accounts open and close, policies are taken out, LPAs are registered, wills are amended, significant gifts are made. We review the booklet as part of your ongoing planning relationship — typically at your annual review — to make sure the information remains accurate and complete.

Download the booklet below, complete it with your adviser, and store it somewhere your executor will be able to find it. Then tell your executor it exists.

How probate works

Probate is the legal process that gives your executor the authority to deal with your estate. Without it, most financial institutions will not release funds, and property cannot be transferred. Understanding what it involves — and how long it takes — is one of the most practically useful things an executor can know in advance.

Step 1: Register the death and obtain the death certificate

A death must be registered within five days in England and Wales. The death certificate is the document that unlocks almost everything that follows — banks, pension providers, HMRC, and the probate registry all require it. Request several certified copies at registration; you will need them.

Step 2: Locate the will and notify the executors

The executor named in the will has the legal authority to act — but that authority is not automatic. It comes from the grant of probate. In the meantime, the executor can take immediate steps: arranging the funeral, securing property, and beginning to gather information about assets and liabilities. This is where the My Estate booklet does most of its work. An executor who knows where the will is, who the key contacts are, and what accounts exist can begin immediately rather than spending weeks on basic detective work.

Step 3: Value the estate

The executor must identify and value all assets as at the date of death: property (requiring a formal RICS valuation), bank and investment accounts, pensions, insurance policies, business interests, personal possessions. At the same time, all debts must be identified — mortgages, credit cards, outstanding bills, tax owed. The net figure is the taxable estate.

Step 4: Calculate and pay any inheritance tax

If the estate exceeds the nil-rate bands, IHT at 40% is due within six months of death — before the grant of probate is issued. This creates a practical problem: the estate cannot be distributed until probate is granted, but the tax must be paid first. The solution in most cases is to use funds held directly in the deceased’s bank accounts (which some banks will release for IHT payment before probate), or to take a short-term loan against the estate. Your financial adviser and solicitor should be involved in this planning before death, not after.

“IHT is due within six months of death. Probate is rarely granted in under three months. The tax has to be paid before the money can be accessed. This is one of the most common practical shocks executors face.”

Step 5: Apply for the grant of probate

The executor submits a probate application to HMCTS, along with the original will, the death certificate, and the completed IHT return. If IHT is due, evidence that it has been paid (or that an arrangement is in place) is also required. The grant of probate is then issued — this is the document that financial institutions and the Land Registry will accept as authority to act. Processing currently takes between eight and sixteen weeks, though complex estates or errors in the application take longer.

Step 6: Collect assets and settle debts

With the grant in hand, the executor can contact each institution in turn, present the grant, and either close accounts and collect balances, or transfer assets directly to beneficiaries. Property is transferred via the Land Registry. Business interests are dealt with separately, often requiring specialist legal advice. All outstanding debts — utility bills, credit cards, loans, income tax due up to the date of death — must be settled before any distribution is made to beneficiaries.

Step 7: Prepare the estate accounts and distribute

The executor prepares a final set of estate accounts showing all assets collected, all debts paid, and the net amount available for distribution. These are shared with beneficiaries before distribution is made. The executor then distributes the estate in accordance with the will. If any beneficiary cannot be located, or disputes arise, the executor may need to retain funds pending resolution. Once everything is settled, the executor’s duties are complete.

How long does the whole process take?

A straightforward estate with one property, a small number of accounts and no IHT complications typically takes six to twelve months end to end. Estates with property that needs to be sold, business interests, overseas assets, disputes, or complex IHT calculations routinely take eighteen months to three years. The single biggest factor within the executor’s control is the quality and completeness of the information they start with.

“The estates that move quickly are the ones where someone has done exactly what this booklet asks: written it down, kept it updated, and told the executor where to find it.”

What about estates without a will?

When someone dies without a will, there is no executor — there is instead an administrator, appointed by the court. The equivalent of the grant of probate is called letters of administration. The process of applying is similar, but there is an additional step of establishing who has the right to administer the estate under the intestacy rules, which can be contested and slow. The administrator has no will to guide distribution and must follow the statutory intestacy rules exactly, regardless of what the deceased might have wanted.

Xentum Sport · In the news

Bryan Robson co-founded
Xentum Sport. Here’s why.

Xentum Sport
• 5 min read
• March 2025

The Daily Mail ran a piece this week on Bryan Robson — England captain, Manchester United legend — and his mission to protect professional footballers from financial ruin. What the article doesn’t spell out: Robson co-founded Xentum Sport because of what he’s personally been through. This is that story.

DM
Daily Mail · Original article
How Bryan Robson is warning Man United stars about the dangers of ‘evil artists and opportunistic chancers’
↗
40%
of professional footballers go bankrupt within five years of retiring
£250k
lost by Robson to a hotel investment that turned out not to exist
£550k
lost in an HMRC tax case that proper planning would have prevented

He’s been stung himself.
That’s the point.

Bryan Robson is not a spokesman for a financial planning firm. He is a co-founder of one. He built Xentum Sport alongside Simon Andrews — a former Manchester United apprentice who became a Chartered Financial Planner — because he got fed up of watching teammates, friends, and former colleagues lose money they should never have lost.

He was defrauded out of £250,000 in a Canadian hotel investment that was never built. He received professional-looking updates, maps, dimensions of the property — and when he tried to get his money back, the hotel didn’t exist. He also lost money in film investment schemes that many footballers of his era used as tax relief vehicles, and faced an HMRC IR35 case over his Manchester United ambassador role that cost him hundreds of thousands more.

“I don’t get why I should pay someone a commission or a percentage of my wealth. The more I save, the more they take even if they’re not doing more. That money should be going to my future, not their bonus.”

Bryan Robson — England & Manchester United, Xentum Sport co-founder

His concern is not abstract. Wes Brown — a teammate — went bankrupt. Chris Smalling is in legal action against his former financial advisers over alleged undisclosed fees. These are not reckless people. They are experienced professionals who trusted the wrong relationships at the wrong time.

Why Robson went to Manchester United
first.

Robson’s first call in building Xentum Sport was to go directly to Manchester United and sit down with INEOS chief finance officer Roger Bell. He wanted to make the case for giving young players practical financial education — not the kind that tells them to save, but the kind that explains what independent advice looks like, why percentage fees are a conflict of interest, and how to check whether an adviser is actually working for them.

His concern about parents acting as advisers is particularly pointed. When Robson signed his first professional deal, his parents came with him. His father was a long-distance lorry driver, his mother a cook. Intelligent, trustworthy people — but not financial specialists. Today, the sums are vastly larger, the structures more complex, and the people around young players are often trying to be advisers without the knowledge or FCA registration to do it properly.

⚠ The basic check every player should make

Any financial adviser working with you in the UK must be FCA-registered. Verify this at register.fca.org.uk before any conversation goes further. Registration is necessary but not sufficient — ask every adviser to explain their fee model, any commissions they receive, and any conflicts of interest, in writing, before you agree to anything.

What Xentum Sport was
built to fix.

Robson’s experience led him to one specific structural conclusion: the percentage fee model is a conflict of interest that nobody talks about openly enough. An adviser charging 1% of assets under management on a £3m portfolio earns £30,000 a year from that client — regardless of how much work they do, whether markets go up or down, or whether the advice is genuinely in the client’s interest. The more you save, the more they earn. That incentive shapes advice in ways that are legal, common, and rarely examined.

Xentum Sport operates on fixed fees only. The fee is agreed in advance, in pounds, before any work begins. It does not change if your portfolio grows. It does not earn more if you buy a particular product. And it does not vary based on who refers you. The advice is shaped entirely by what the plan requires — not by what generates the most income for us.

  • Fixed fees agreed in advance — you know the cost before any conversation begins
  • No commission from any product, platform, or investment provider
  • No percentage of earnings or assets — ever
  • FCA-regulated Chartered Financial Planners, not generalist advisers
  • Specialist experience in footballer finances — image rights, IR35, short career planning, sudden wealth
  • Planning built around your career timeline, not a standard retirement model

The questions you should be able
to answer right now.

If you are a professional footballer currently working with a financial adviser — or considering one — you should be able to answer all of the following without having to check:

  • What is the total annual cost of my financial advice, in pounds — not as a percentage?
  • Does my adviser earn anything from the products or platforms they recommend?
  • Is my adviser FCA-registered, and are they independent or tied to specific providers?
  • Have I structured my image rights correctly, with current HMRC compliance documentation?
  • If my career ended tomorrow through injury, what income would I have and for how long?
  • Do I have a financial plan that accounts for a career that might end before I’m 35?
  • Who is the named beneficiary on my pension and life insurance — and is it still correct?

If any of those produce uncertainty, that is not a failing — it is information. Robson’s mission, and ours, is to make sure those questions have clear answers before they become expensive ones.

Xentum Corporate · Tax Planning

SEIS, EIS, and VCTs:
the tax tools most business owners ignore.

If you’re running a profitable business and paying 45p in tax on every pound you draw above £125,140, there are government-backed schemes that can change that materially. Most business owners either don’t know they exist or assume they’re too complicated to be worth it.

Xentum Corporate
• 7 min read
• 2025/26 tax year

The government has created a set of investment schemes specifically designed to encourage capital into early-stage and growing businesses. In return, investors receive meaningful tax relief. For business owners who are already comfortable with risk and who pay tax at the highest rate, these schemes deserve serious attention.

This article is not a product recommendation. It is an explanation of how these schemes work, who they are typically suited to, and the questions you should be asking before considering them as part of a broader financial plan. Used well, they can reduce a significant tax bill. Used badly — or with the wrong provider — they carry real risk that needs to be understood clearly.

The four schemes,
at a glance.

There are four main government-backed tax-efficient investment schemes relevant to business owners. Each targets a different type of investor and a different stage of business risk.

VCT
Venture Capital Trust
30% income tax relief · tax-free dividends
You invest in a listed trust that holds stakes in qualifying early-stage companies. You receive 30% income tax relief on up to £200,000 invested per tax year, dividends are tax-free, and any growth is exempt from CGT. Widely used by business owners who want to reduce their income tax bill each year without taking direct company risk.
EIS
Enterprise Investment Scheme
30% income tax relief · CGT deferral
Direct investment into qualifying unquoted companies. 30% income tax relief on up to £1m invested per year (£2m if targeting knowledge-intensive companies). CGT deferral if proceeds from another gain are reinvested. If the shares are held for three years and the company qualifies, any gain on disposal is also free of CGT.
SEIS
Seed Enterprise Investment Scheme
50% income tax relief · CGT exemption
The highest-relief scheme, designed for investment into the very earliest-stage companies. 50% income tax relief on up to £200,000 invested per year. Any gain on qualifying shares held for three or more years is entirely exempt from CGT. The risk profile is higher — seed-stage companies have a high failure rate — but so is the relief available to offset it.
Business Relief
Business Property Relief
100% IHT exemption after 2 years
Not a growth investment — rather an IHT planning tool. Qualifying shares in unquoted trading companies are fully exempt from inheritance tax after two years of ownership. Unlike trusts or gifting (which require seven years), business relief qualifies in two. Capital is preserved and accessible. Widely used post-exit to replace the IHT exemption that a trading business previously provided.

Who these schemes are
typically suited to.

These are not mainstream investments. They carry genuine risk, they are illiquid, and the tax reliefs are only available if specific conditions are met and maintained. But for the right person, they solve a real problem.

VCTs are most commonly used by business owners and higher earners who have a regular income tax problem — drawing profits from a business each year and paying 45% on everything above the additional rate threshold. The 30% income tax relief works on a pound-for-pound basis against your tax bill. If you invest £50,000 into a VCT, you receive £15,000 back against your income tax liability for that year. Dividends from VCTs are then tax-free, so the investment continues to work tax-efficiently in subsequent years.

EIS and SEIS are more suitable when there is a specific gain to shelter — from a property sale, business disposal, or investment realisation — or when a client is prepared to take direct, concentrated risk in early-stage companies for a meaningful tax benefit. SEIS in particular, at 50% relief, is hard to replicate through any other legitimate mechanism. A £100,000 SEIS investment effectively costs £50,000 after relief, and if the company succeeds and shares are sold after three years, all of that gain is exempt from CGT.

Business Relief becomes particularly relevant post-exit. When a founder sells their business, they lose the IHT exemption their trading company provided. The proceeds — often sitting in cash or a general investment portfolio — become fully liable to 40% inheritance tax. Business Relief investments replace that exemption within two years, without requiring a trust structure or seven-year survival period.

The post-exit window

The period immediately after a business sale is when these tools are most powerful — and most overlooked. A founder has just crystallised a large gain (potentially subject to CGT), is sitting on a large cash sum (now fully IHT-exposed), and has lost the tax sheltering effect their trading company provided. EIS for CGT deferral, Business Relief for IHT planning, and VCTs for ongoing income tax reduction can all work together during this window. This is exactly why pre-exit planning matters: having these structures identified before the sale completes gives you significantly more flexibility than starting from scratch afterwards.

The honest risks
you need to understand.

These schemes exist because the government wants capital directed into risky, early-stage businesses. That risk is real. It is not a technicality on a factsheet — it is the reason the reliefs are generous in the first place.

SchemeMain riskLiquidityMinimum hold
VCTCompany failure within the trust; market price below NAVListed, but secondary market is thin5 years (or relief is clawed back)
EISCompany failure; qualifying status lostIlliquid — no listed market3 years (or relief is clawed back)
SEISVery high failure rate at seed stageHighly illiquid3 years (or relief is clawed back)
Business ReliefRegulatory changes to qualifying status; investment risk in underlying assetsAccess typically after 12 months; withdrawal possible but fund dependent2 years for IHT exemption

A further risk specific to Business Relief: the FCA classifies these investments as high risk at the company level, regardless of the quality of assets underneath. This means that when a recommendation is made to a client, the risk warning will say “you could lose all of your money.” That warning is technically accurate and legally required — but it does not distinguish between a well-managed fund with institutional-grade assets and diversified contracted revenues, and a poorly run one with concentrated, speculative positions. Understanding what is actually under the bonnet matters enormously in this space.

⚠ Provider due diligence is not optional

The quality of providers in this space varies considerably. Questions to ask before recommending or investing in any BR, VCT, EIS, or SEIS product include: What is the track record of the investment team? What does the underlying portfolio consist of? How is liquidity managed? Is the fund diversified across asset types, or concentrated in a single sector? Are the underlying assets contracted, real assets with strong counterparties — or speculative positions? For Business Relief specifically, has the qualifying status been confirmed by HMRC and maintained consistently? These are not box-ticking questions. They are the difference between a solid recommendation and an expensive mistake.

How these tools fit into
a broader plan.

None of these schemes should be considered in isolation. They are tax planning tools, not investment strategies in their own right. The right question is never “should I invest in a VCT?” — it is “given my tax position, my time horizon, my exit plans, and my existing portfolio, does a VCT make sense as part of a broader structure?”

For most Xentum Corporate clients — business owners who are one to five years from an exit — the relevant questions are:

  • ✓Am I drawing profits from the business and paying income tax at 45%? If yes, VCTs may reduce that bill meaningfully each year.
  • ✓Do I have a capital gain — from a property sale, investment disposal, or partial business exit — that I want to defer or shelter? EIS may provide the mechanism.
  • ✓Am I approaching or post-exit with a large cash sum that is now fully IHT-exposed? Business Relief may replace the exemption the trading company provided, within two years.
  • ✓Am I comfortable taking direct, early-stage company risk for a 50% tax relief? SEIS may be appropriate — but only as a small proportion of an overall portfolio.

The answers to those questions determine whether and how these tools belong in a plan — and in what combination. They also determine the order: for someone approaching a sale, identifying these structures before the transaction completes is significantly more valuable than attempting to retrofit them afterwards.

A note on the 2025/26 landscape

Business Relief is seeing increased demand as a result of two specific legislative changes. The April 2027 pension reform — which will bring pension assets into the IHT estate for the first time — is dragging many people into IHT liability who previously were not exposed. And the reduction in AIM market relief (from 100% to 50%) has pushed more advisers and clients toward unquoted Business Relief as the cleaner, better-established alternative. These are not abstract regulatory shifts — they have a direct, calculable impact on the IHT position of clients who hold significant pension and investment assets.

Does this belong
in your plan?

These are not off-the-shelf products. Whether VCT, EIS, SEIS, or Business Relief belongs in your financial plan depends entirely on your tax position, your timeline, and your broader objectives. Start with a conversation.

Quick reference
VCT: 30% relief, £200k limit, income tax
EIS: 30% relief, £1m limit, CGT deferral
SEIS: 50% relief, £200k limit, highest risk
BR: 100% IHT exemption after 2 years

We work with athletes at different stages — from young professionals on their first significant contract to those with established wealth approaching or past the end of their career. What matters is that you're ready to put a proper plan in place, not the size of your contract.
How is Xentum Sport different from a regular financial adviser?
Most financial advisers serve a broad range of clients and have limited experience of the specific pressures athletes face: short career windows, irregular income, tax on image rights and bonuses, agent relationships, and the psychological challenge of life after sport. We've built a service specifically for this context. Our fee model is also fixed — not a percentage of what you have. That means our advice is focused on what's right for you, not on managing as much of your money as possible.
What does a first conversation look like?
It's a straightforward call — usually 30–45 minutes. We listen to where you are, what you're trying to sort out, and whether we're the right fit. There's no charge, no paperwork, and no obligation to proceed. If we're not the right option for you, we'll say so and point you in the right direction.
Can my agent or parent join the conversation?
Yes — we're used to working with families of young professionals and are happy to include agents or parents where that's helpful. That said, the financial plan is always built around you and what you need — not around what's most convenient for the people around you.
Fees and how we charge
Why do you charge a fixed fee instead of a percentage of what I have?
Because a percentage model creates an incentive to manage as much of your money as possible — not to give you the best advice. If we charge 1% of £3m, we earn £30,000 per year whether we do good work or not. A fixed fee means we earn what we charge regardless of your portfolio size. It also gives you cost certainty, which matters when you're planning for a career that has a defined endpoint. As Chris Smalling put it: knowing your adviser isn't taking a percentage of your future gives you real confidence that they're working for you.
How much does it cost?
Our WealthPlan™ is £2,495. Our ongoing service starts from £3,000 per year depending on the complexity of your situation. The full pricing calculator — which shows exactly what you'd pay before any conversation — is on the fees page. See the pricing calculator →
Do you charge separately for investment management?
No. Our ongoing annual fee covers investment management — we don't add a separate layer of charges for managing your portfolio. You'll pay platform fees (charged directly by the platform, not by us) and fund management charges (built into the fund price), but no additional Xentum investment management fee on top of your annual advice fee.
Financial planning for athletes
When is the right time to start financial planning in my career?
As early as possible. The most valuable financial decisions happen at the start of a career — when you first have significant earnings, when you make your first property purchase, when you structure your tax affairs. Athletes who wait until they're 30 to engage a financial planner have typically missed several of the highest-leverage moments. The compounding effect of good early decisions is significant.
What happens to my money when my career ends?
That's exactly what we plan for. Your WealthPlan™ models your entire financial life — not just your playing years. We'll look at how much you need to have accumulated by the time your career ends to support the life you want beyond sport, what passive income your investments can generate, how your property fits into that picture, and what your pension looks like. Life after sport is the goal. We help you build towards it from day one.
Can you help with image rights and tax planning?
Yes — athletes often have complex tax situations involving image rights companies, multiple income streams, and offshore considerations. We work with specialist tax advisers and accountants in this area to ensure your planning is coordinated. We won't give you specific tax advice beyond our regulated remit — that's the accountant's job — but we'll make sure the right professionals are involved and that your financial plan accounts for the tax picture properly.
Do you work with family members too?
Yes. Many of our athlete clients involve family members in their planning — whether that's a partner, parents who have helped with early financial decisions, or siblings. We're comfortable working across a family context where that's helpful. Our starting point is always the athlete's own financial plan, but we can extend planning to family members where needed.
