Xentum Family · FAQs

Questions from
families like yours.

The most common questions we hear from individuals and families before they start a WealthPlan™. Honest answers, no jargon.

Getting started
How do I know if I need a financial planner?
A useful test: do you know whether your current financial arrangements will support the life you want in retirement? Do you know whether you could retire earlier than planned? Do you have a clear view of your inheritance tax exposure? If any of these feel uncertain, a financial planner adds real value. Most people don't need a financial planner for simple situations — but most people's situations are more complex than they realise, particularly when property, multiple pensions, children, and estate planning are all in the mix.
What's the minimum amount of money you need to work with Xentum?
We don't have a hard minimum, but our fixed fee structure means we're typically better value for clients with investable assets above £150,000. Below that level, a percentage-based adviser may actually be cheaper — and we'll tell you that honestly if it applies to you. We'd rather not take on clients where we're not the most cost-effective option.
Can couples do a WealthPlan™ together?
Yes — in fact, we strongly encourage it. One of the most valuable parts of the WealthPlan™ process is the Grab Life Wheel, where both partners complete the exercise independently. The results are almost always different, and the conversation that follows — about what each person actually wants from life — is frequently one of the most useful conversations couples have had in years. Financial planning works far better when both people are involved.
I already have a financial adviser. How do I know if I should switch?
Three questions worth asking your current adviser: Can you show me a cashflow model of my financial life over the next 30 years? Is your advice fully independent (whole of market)? Can you confirm in writing exactly what I'm paying and what that covers? If you can't get clear answers to all three, it's worth having a conversation with us. We're happy to do a no-obligation review — not to tell you to switch, but to help you assess whether your current arrangement is working as well as it could.
What financial planning covers
What does a WealthPlan™ actually cover?
Your full balance sheet, a lifetime cashflow model, retirement income strategy, tax planning (ISAs, pensions, CGT, IHT), investment recommendations, protection gap analysis, estate planning, and a prioritised written action list. It's not a generic template — it's built around your specific situation, your goals from the Grab Life Wheel exercise, and the scenarios you want to stress-test. See the full WealthPlan™ process →
Do you manage investments as well as give advice?
Yes. Investment management is included within our ongoing annual fee — there's no separate charge for this. We don't charge a percentage of assets for investment management, which is one of the ways our fixed fee model creates better alignment. We use evidence-based investment approaches with low underlying fund costs, and your portfolio is managed in line with your WealthPlan™ strategy.
Do you help with mortgage advice?
Mortgage advice falls outside our core scope, but we can refer you to specialist mortgage advisers within our professional network. Property decisions — whether to buy, remortgage, downsize, or release equity — absolutely feature in your WealthPlan™ from a strategic perspective. We'll model the impact of different property decisions on your overall financial plan.
Can you help with estate planning and inheritance tax?
Yes — IHT and estate planning is a core part of what we do, particularly for clients who have accumulated significant wealth or who own property. We'll model your estate value, identify IHT exposure, and recommend strategies — gifting, trust structures, pension planning, life insurance — to manage it. For complex estate matters requiring trust documentation or legal advice, we work alongside your solicitor.
Retirement planning
When should I start planning for retirement?
The honest answer: the earlier the better, because compounding works over long timeframes. But many of our most valuable client relationships start when people are in their 40s or 50s — close enough to retirement to make the planning feel urgent, but far enough away to make real changes. Even if you're 10 or 15 years from retirement, the decisions you make now will have a significant impact on the income and flexibility you have then.
How much money do I need to retire?
It depends entirely on the life you want to live. Our WealthPlan™ process starts by getting clear on what that looks like — not in financial terms, but in human terms. What does your ideal week in retirement look like? What would you spend? Where would you live? What does long-term care provision look like for you? Once we know that, we can model the number with reasonable precision. The number most people need is different from what they assume.

Xentum Corporate · FAQs

The questions founders
actually ask us.

Collected from real prospect and client conversations in 2025 and 2026 — in their own words. If your question isn’t here, drop Ed a line at [email protected].

The process
“In terms of helping me make a decision, how does this process actually work?”

We run a two-meeting process within 30 days.

Discovery Meeting — this is about understanding you, not just the business. We start with the Grab Life exercise, exploring what matters most to you at this stage of life and how you want your time, energy, and attention spent. We also discuss your family values, financial objectives, your current position (assets, liabilities, income, spending, and how dependent your lifestyle is on the business), and what a “good outcome” actually looks like.

Strategy Meeting — within 30 days of the Discovery Meeting, we prepare and present clearly modelled scenarios: exiting now, exiting later, partial exit or de-risking, and continuing to run the business. For each option we explore how your lifestyle and family position would change, the risks you’d be taking or avoiding, and the financial and personal trade-offs. This is where uncertainty is replaced with clarity.

A written report summarising the discussion, assumptions, and conclusions is delivered within 3–5 working days. From there, three routes are possible — and all are valid: no further relationship, Exit Stewardship only, or Exit Stewardship alongside investment management and financial advice.

“What if I’ve already made a decision?”

The two-meeting process is an important starting point on your exit journey whether you’ve made a decision or not. It helps you become clear on what life looks like post-exit and is the starting point for building out your financial plan. The process takes the same time and resources from the Xentum team, so we charge in the same way regardless.

“What if I don’t want to fully exit — could I sell part and stay involved?”

The initial piece of fixed-fee consultancy work is designed to help you become unstuck in your decision-making and create clarity on which route is best for you. We are entirely agnostic as to which route you decide is right — full exit, partial exit, or staying in. Our role is to give you the tools to make the decision with confidence, not to steer you in any particular direction.

“What kind of notice do you need if we want to get started?”

We typically have capacity to work with around two new business owners each month, and that capacity will grow as the team grows. For the first meeting, we can usually book with a 3–5 day turnaround if diaries allow — there isn’t much prep required, it’s simply about having a great conversation in a relaxed setting. The Strategy Meeting is then booked within 30 days of the first.

Fees
“How do you charge for it?”

Everything is fixed-fee and agreed in advance. There are no percentage charges, no hidden costs, and no commission from any product or investment we recommend.

  • The Exit Decision — £2,495 + VAT. A one-off fixed fee for the two-meeting process, payable upfront before the first meeting. This is a deductible business expense.
  • Exit Stewardship — £250/month + VAT. Paid monthly in advance by direct debit. A deductible business expense.
  • WealthPlan™ (ongoing) — one of four tiers: £250, £500, £825, or £1,250 per month.
  • Initial product and investment advice — a fixed fee depending on the scope, with an estimate provided as early as possible.
“The £2,495 is your plan — but how else do you make money on what we do?”

That’s the honest version of a question we hear a lot. The £2,495 covers the Exit Decision process. After that, if you engage us for Exit Stewardship, that’s £250/month. If you want us to manage your investments and financial planning on an ongoing basis post-exit, that’s the WealthPlan™ service, charged at one of four fixed monthly tiers. At no point do we charge a percentage of your wealth or earn commission from products. We have no financial interest in how much you invest or which products you choose — only in doing a good job.

Working with other advisers
“How do you work with a corporate finance adviser?”

We have distinct roles. Our role is to provide a framework for your personal finances so you can make a confident decision about whether exiting is right for you, and to sit alongside you as offers take shape — building and refining your financial plan in real time. We also help you think about what comes next before the event, so it doesn’t feel like a sudden transition. The corporate finance adviser’s role is to understand the value of your business, identify your options, and find the best deal on the market. Corporate finance professionals introduce clients to us because they want the people they take to market to be confident and committed — knowing they’ve made a personal decision they can stand behind.

“Do you give advice on the cash and investments once the deal is done?”

Yes. At our heart, Xentum is an independent financial planning firm. We provide specific exit consultancy services for business owners, but we also provide ongoing financial planning and investment management post-exit — advising on what to do with upfront cash, earn-out proceeds, and seller-financed deal payments as they arrive. We have a sports team and a family team that do the same for clients in those areas.

“So you work with our legal and tax advisers rather than bringing your own to the table?”

We work closely with a network of specialists across corporate finance, M&A law, debt advisory, business coaching, and due diligence. If you already have your own advisers, we’ll work closely with them to provide the best outcome. We don’t have in-house corporate finance advisers, accountants, or tax advisers — we sit alongside them, not instead of them.

Logistics & practicalities
“Where are you based? Can we meet in person?”

Xentum is based in Cheshire, around 30 minutes from Manchester, with meeting room space in Knutsford and Warrington. We also look after clients in London (with regular trips to the capital), and as far as Hull, Lincoln, Glasgow, and Kent. For the Discovery Meeting in particular, we think face-to-face matters — and we’ll travel to see prospective clients we think are a good fit. We use Microsoft Teams for video calls where convenience works better.

“Would you see me and my husband/partner together or as individual clients?”

Together, wherever possible. Great financial planning is done together — dreaming big together, navigating the hard decisions together, and setting the course of the family as one. We believe both parties should be present as much as possible. One of the most valuable moments in the process is when both partners complete the Grab Life exercise independently and compare the results — the differences are often revealing, and the conversation that follows is almost always one of the most useful a couple has had in years.

“How long has Xentum been operating?”

Dominic founded Xentum in 2004, so we’re into our 22nd year serving clients. We achieved Chartered status as a firm midway through that journey — a standard held by around 15% of UK financial advice firms — and continue to hold it. We’re proud to have built a business that will still be here, still improving, in another 22 years.

Bigger questions
“When you say ‘plan’, what do you actually mean?”

We believe in the value of financial planning and its ability to help people make consistently great decisions — ones that enhance their wellbeing and enjoyment of life. The plan itself matters, but the process of planning matters more. Like a business plan, the original document can be dead in the water within days. But the underlying process — if it’s quick, focused, and reviewed regularly — is what allows you to decide on strategy and take action. That’s what we’re building with you.

“I’ve also got to think about inheritance tax — what’s the best vehicle to manage it all?”

Inheritance tax is a consideration for most of our clients — very few are content for HMRC to take 40% of wealth they’ve spent 15–20 years building. Recent changes to business asset relief have made it increasingly important for business owners to think about the best strategies in advance of a sale, working alongside a tax adviser. The right structure depends on your long-term family objectives — and that conversation starts with understanding what those objectives actually are, which is exactly what the Grab Life exercise is designed to surface. You can also use our IHT calculator below to model your current exposure.

“The terminology is difficult to remember — is that going to be a problem?”

Not at all. One of the most honest things a prospect has ever said to us, and it captures something we hear often. If we don’t communicate in language you understand, we’re not doing our job. We aim to simplify things as much as possible — using language and analogies that land rather than confuse. Ask as many questions as you need to. That’s what we’re here for.

Xentum Sport · Tax

Your agent fees are
probably a tax liability.

Xentum Sport
• 6 min read
• 2025/26

HMRC recovered £67.5 million in extra tax from football clubs, players, and agents in just one year. It opened investigations into 83 players and 20 clubs. The primary target: agent fees paid by clubs that should have been declared as a taxable benefit in kind by the player. If your agent was paid by your club during a transfer or contract negotiation — and you didn’t declare it — you may have a problem.

What is a ‘dual representation’
contract?

When a player moves clubs or signs a new contract, the agent involved often claims to represent both the player and the buying club. This is known as dual representation. The club pays the agent’s fee — typically a large one — and that payment gets split between services provided to the club and services provided to the player.

For years, the standard industry practice was to split the fee 50/50 between club and player. The club deducts its half as a business expense for corporation tax purposes. The player’s half, if paid by the club on the player’s behalf, should technically be declared as a benefit in kind — taxable income. In practice, many clubs and players have not declared it correctly. That is what HMRC is now pursuing aggressively.

“When the club pays a large proportion of an agent’s fee, it amounts to a benefit in kind paid to the player — on which income tax is due.”

UHY Hacker Young, reporting on HMRC’s 2024 crackdown

Why the 50/50 split
no longer works.

In May 2024, HMRC published new guidance on dual representation contracts that changes the landscape significantly. HMRC’s starting position is now that the agent primarily works for the player — not the club. That means the default assumption is that the agent’s fee is almost entirely for the player’s benefit, and any portion paid by the club should be treated as a benefit in kind taxable on the player.

The 50/50 split that was widespread industry practice is no longer acceptable as a default. HMRC now requires clubs and agents to provide specific evidence — detailed records of what services were actually provided to the club — to justify any portion of the fee being attributed to the club rather than the player. Without that evidence, HMRC will treat the full amount as taxable income of the player.

⚠ What this means in numbers

If your agent secured you a £10m contract and charged a £1m fee — paid entirely by the club under a dual representation arrangement — and no proper records exist to justify a club/player split, HMRC could treat the full £1m as a benefit in kind. At 45% income tax plus 2% employee NI, that is a personal tax bill of £470,000 on a fee you didn’t receive in cash. The club also faces Class 1A NIC of 13.8% — another £138,000 — which it may try to recover from you.

What HMRC is looking for
and who is being investigated.

HMRC has been explicit that it views the football industry as a priority target. In the year to March 2024 alone it recovered £67.5m — part of £384m collected over five years from investigations into clubs, players, and agents. It is not just Premier League clubs. HMRC has issued enquiry notices to clubs across the football pyramid, many of which have fallen into arrears with tax payments as a result.

The investigations are triggered by a range of factors: agent fees that appear disproportionate to the services documented, transfers where the fee allocation lacks commercial justification, arrangements involving family members acting as agents, and cases where payments went through “shadow” agents before reaching the registered agent. HMRC is particularly focused on young players — often signing first professional contracts at wages above £150,000 — who may not even know they are required to file a self-assessment tax return.

The international athlete
complication.

From 6 April 2025, the UK’s remittance basis of taxation has been abolished and replaced with a new foreign income and gains (FIG) regime. For international footballers playing in the Premier League, this introduces new complexity. The FIG regime offers a four-year exemption for foreign income — but it explicitly excludes performance income. That means match fees, media appearances, sponsorship, and image rights deals derived from playing in the UK are fully subject to UK taxation regardless of where the player is domiciled.

The reformed overseas workday relief may provide some mitigation for non-UK duties, but the interaction with agent fees and benefit-in-kind charges requires careful analysis. Players who have previously used the remittance basis may also want to consider the Temporary Repatriation Facility, which allows previously unremitted foreign income and gains to be brought into the UK at a reduced rate of 12% for 2025/26 and 2026/27.

What you should be doing
right now.

If any of the following apply to you, this requires immediate attention:

  • Your agent has been paid partly or fully by your club in any transfer or contract negotiation
  • You have not checked whether those payments were correctly reported on form P11D
  • You have never filed a self-assessment tax return despite earnings above £100,000
  • You have image rights arrangements that have not been reviewed in the last two years
  • You are an international player who was using the remittance basis before April 2025
  • A family member has acted as your agent or intermediary in any deal

The time to deal with this is before HMRC raises an enquiry, not after. Voluntary disclosure and proactive engagement with HMRC typically result in significantly lower penalties than being on the receiving end of a compliance check. The cost of a proper tax review is a fraction of the cost of an HMRC investigation.

Not sure where
you stand?

A confidential conversation with a Xentum Sport planner. We’ll help you understand your exposure and connect you with the right tax specialists if needed.

Cash Out With Confidence · Book 2
Value, Sufficiency, and the Number That Actually Matters
Xentum Corporate · Ed Stubbs, Chartered Financial Planner
Start here
Chapters
Close
Introduction

The Most Dangerous Question in an Exit

If you're reading this, you've probably had a number in your head for years.

You might know where it came from. A competitor who sold. A figure someone mentioned at a dinner. A multiple you read somewhere, applied to your own profits late one night.

Or maybe you don't know where it came from. Maybe it's just there — a round figure, a milestone, a line in the sand you drew a long time ago without ever checking whether it was in the right place.

You know your margins. You know your sector. You could talk someone through your P&L without opening a file.

And yet, if someone asked you — not what your business is worth, but what it needs to be worth for you to walk away and never worry again — most founders at this stage would pause.

Some would say a number. Few could explain why that number is the right one.

This isn't because you haven't thought about it. It's because the question you've been answering for 20 years is the wrong one.

"What is my business worth?" is a market question. "What does it need to be worth for me?" is a life question.

They sound similar. They are not the same question. And the gap between them is where exits go wrong.

This book is not about maximising price.

It's about understanding what your business needs to be worth — and why most founders never define it properly.

If you've ever caught yourself thinking:

  • "I'll know if it's enough when I see the offer"
  • "I've always said I'd sell at the right number"
  • "I worked it out based on what someone else got"
  • "I know my numbers, I just don't know what they mean for me personally"

Then this book is for you.

Offers don't create clarity — they test whether clarity already exists. And if it doesn't, the number that arrives rarely feels like enough, regardless of what it is.

Chapter 1

Why 'How Much?' Feels Obvious (And Isn't)

Most founders approaching an exit feel like they've already answered this question.

They've talked about value for years. They've heard what businesses in their space go for. They've done the multiplication in their head — profit times a number, arrived at a figure, filed it away as roughly right.

Some have spoken to a broker. Some have had a valuation done. Some have watched a competitor sell and reverse-engineered the maths from Companies House.

It feels like preparation. And it is — just for the wrong question.

Most founders have prepared answers for the question, "what is my business worth?"

Almost none have prepared answers for, "what does it need to be worth for me to live the life I actually want?"

Those are different questions. And the distance between them is where the discomfort is.

Where the Number Comes From

Most people think they arrived at their number through analysis. In practice, the number arrived at them.

A founder hears that a business in their sector sold for seven times earnings. That figure enters the bloodstream. Every subsequent calculation orbits it.

Someone at a conference mentions they got five million. That becomes the floor.

A broker gives a range — three to five — and the lower end is immediately forgotten.

The first number you hear becomes the reference point for every number that follows. Not because it's accurate. Because it was first.

This is how the brain handles uncertainty. When a question is difficult — and "what is my business worth?" is genuinely difficult — the mind reaches for the nearest available figure and adjusts from there.

But the adjustment is almost never far enough.

You anchor to what you heard. You adjust a little. And you call it your own view.

But it isn't your view. It's someone else's deal, someone else's context, someone else's life — dressed up as your number.

Why Comparison Makes It Worse

Founders don't think about value in isolation. They think about it relative to someone they know.

The one who sold a similar business. The one who got a number that felt high. The one they played golf or cricket or padel with, who mentioned a figure that stuck.

The difficulty is that every comparison is missing context.

The business that sold for nine times was forty times larger, with a diversified client base, a deep management team, and a buyer who needed the acquisition to complete a platform play. None of that applies to a two-person niche operation doing seven hundred thousand in profit.

But the multiple travels without the context. And once it lands, it distorts everything.

Founders who compare upward — to someone who got more, in a different situation — reliably feel worse about their own outcome, even when their outcome comfortably funds the life they want.

This is one of the most consistent findings in the psychology of decision-making: satisfaction is not determined by what you receive. It's determined by the gap between what you receive and what you expected.

And expectations are almost always set by someone else's number.

The Peak-Year Trap

There's a quieter version of the same distortion.

A founder who's had a strong year — their best year, the year it all came together — naturally anchors their sense of value to that peak.

This year's profit becomes the baseline. Anything below it feels like decline.

But acquirers don't price peak years. They price normalised earnings. They look at three years, sometimes five, smooth out the anomalies, and arrive at a figure that reflects what the business reliably produces — not what it produced once, in ideal conditions, with everything running perfectly.

The gap between the founder's anchor — the best year — and the buyer's anchor — the average year — is where valuation arguments begin. And where emotional damage is done.

Because the founder doesn't experience the buyer's adjustment as rational pricing. They experience it as undervaluation. As disrespect. As someone failing to see what this business really is.

It isn't. It's two people looking at the same business from different positions — one from inside, where the best year feels like the truth, and one from outside, where the average year is all that can be relied upon.

The question this chapter leaves you with

"Is the number in my head actually mine — or did it arrive from somewhere else, carrying someone else's context, someone else's life, and someone else's risk profile?"

Until that's answered honestly, every valuation will feel either too low or suspiciously high.

Chapter 2

The Illusion of the Big Number

There's a moment in almost every exit conversation where a number lands.

It might come from a broker. A valuation. A back-of-envelope calculation. An offer.

Whatever the source, the number arrives as a single, clean figure. Six million. Four and a half. Eight.

And the brain registers it as real.

But the number on the page is not the number that reaches your life.

By the time it has been taxed, structured, staged, and eroded, the amount that actually lands — available, liquid, yours — is materially different from the figure you heard first.

This chapter is about what sits between the headline and the reality.

Gross Is Not Net

Capital gains tax removes a percentage of the headline before you see a penny. In most founder exits, somewhere between 18% and 24% disappears before anything reaches your account.

Founders who have spent years legitimately minimising tax inside the business are often shocked by the bluntness of the CGT calculation on the way out.

The number you discussed with your broker is gross. The number you live on is net. The gap between them is not a rounding error.

Deferred Isn't Received

Not all sale proceeds arrive at once.

Earn-outs. Staged payments. Deferred consideration tied to conditions. Shares in an acquiring entity with no open market.

Each of these is technically "value." None of them is money that you can spend on the celebration trip to enjoy the fruits of 15+ years of hard work.

A founder with a headline of five million, where two arrives on completion and three is tied to a two-year earn-out, does not have five million. They have two million and three million in promises. And promises are not the same thing as cash.

You've sold. You've handed over. You're no longer in control. And yet the number you were told isn't the number you're holding.

That gap between "sold" and "received" is where anxiety quietly moves in.

The Premium You Carry (That No One Will Pay)

There is one more erosion that doesn't show up in any calculation.

You built this business. Not from an inheritance. Not from a playbook. Probably from nothing.

Years of pricing the work yourself. Years of sleepless months around payroll. Years of carrying it through conditions that would have broken most people.

That experience creates a premium in your head — a sense that the business should be worth more because of what it cost you to build it.

It's understandable. It's human. And the market will not pay for it.

A buyer does not price history. A buyer prices future cash flows, discounted by risk. They don't see the nights or the turnaround or the rescue. They see the next five years of earnings — and how likely those earnings are to materialise without you in the building.

This is what psychologists call effort justification — the more painful the journey, the more valuable the destination must feel. It's consistent, predictable, and universal. It is not a personal failing. It is a feature of how the brain processes sacrifice.

But if you carry that premium into a negotiation, one of two things happens. Either you reject offers that would have given you everything you need. Or you accept and feel quietly robbed — because the number, even if sufficient, doesn't honour the effort.

Both outcomes are avoidable. But only if you separate what the business cost you from what it's worth to someone else.

Why the Headline Triggers Disappointment

There is a neurological reason why this erosion feels worse than it should.

When a founder first hears a headline number — six million, eight million — the brain generates a reward prediction. It anticipates what that number will feel like when it arrives.

But what actually arrives is the net: after tax, after deferrals.

The gap between what the brain anticipated and what landed is experienced not as "reasonable costs" but as loss. The disappointment is proportional to the size of the headline, not the size of the shortfall.

This is why founders who sell for more than they need can still feel deflated. Not because the outcome was bad. But because the headline set an expectation the reality couldn't match.

Daniel Kahneman's work on reference points explains this precisely: satisfaction is not determined by what you receive. It is determined by the gap between what you receive and what you expected.

The headline is the expectation. The net is the reality. And the gap between them is where seller's disappointment is born.

The question this chapter leaves you with

"Once I've subtracted the tax, the deferrals, the structure, and the premium I'm carrying in my head — what number actually reaches my life?"

Until that's answered, every headline feels like a promise. And every net figure feels like a disappointment.

Chapter 3

Three Numbers Every Founder Confuses

Most founders carry one number in their head. A milestone. A target. A figure they'd sell for.

It feels like a clear position. But it isn't one number doing one job.

It's three numbers collapsed into one — undifferentiated, unweighted, and doing the work of all three badly.

The Sufficiency Stack

There are three thresholds that matter in an exit. They serve different purposes. They carry different emotional weight. And confusing them is the single most common reason founders either delay exits they should take or feel dissatisfied by exits they shouldn't.

Threat threshold. Below this, your lifestyle is at risk. You're pulled back into work not by choice but by necessity. This is where the floor gives way.

Lifestyle threshold. This sustains the life you actually want. Not a fantasy life. The life you'd describe honestly — the holidays, the spending, the rhythm that makes you content. This is where worry stops.

Legacy threshold. This is what you'd need to leave something behind. Not maximum inheritance — sufficient inheritance. Enough that the people you care about are supported, without the amount becoming a problem of its own.

Why Separating Them Matters

When these three numbers sit inside a single figure, the figure is almost always too high. Because it's trying to do three jobs at once.

A founder who says "I want five million" is usually saying: I want to know I won't run out. I want to live well without working. I want the kids to be okay.

Three different requirements. Three different price tags. And the first two are almost always lower than the founder assumes — because they've never been separated from the third.

Herbert Simon called this distinction satisficing — the difference between optimising endlessly and identifying the threshold that genuinely meets your needs. Barry Schwartz's later research showed that people who define "enough" before evaluating options are consistently more satisfied with their outcomes than those who keep searching for the best possible result.

The application to exits is direct. A founder who has defined their lifestyle threshold and receives an offer that clears it feels surplus. A founder carrying a single blended number and receiving the same offer feels shortfall.

Same number. Different architecture. Different emotional experience.

Where Founders Get Trapped

The founder whose threat threshold is already met — but who keeps pushing because the other two thresholds are undefined and therefore feel infinite.

The founder whose real driver isn't financial at all — who'd take a discount tomorrow to resolve a family situation cleanly, but can't see that the answer isn't a bigger number, it's a faster one.

And the founder who turned down a reasonable offer years ago — not because it was wrong, but because it "didn't feel like enough." Without the thresholds separated, the number felt insufficient. Not mathematically. Emotionally.

Preparing You for the Next Shift

Once the thresholds are separated, a new question emerges.

If the lifestyle threshold is lower than you assumed, why does your internal valuation remain so high?

That gap is not a maths problem. It's an identity problem. And it's where the next chapter begins.

The question this chapter leaves you with

"Which of the three numbers am I actually trying to reach — and have I ever separated them?"

Until that's done, every figure will carry three jobs and satisfy none of them fully.

Chapter 4

Why Founders Systematically Overvalue Their Business

If overvaluation were a sign of arrogance, this chapter wouldn't exist.

The founders who carry the largest premium in their heads are rarely delusional. They are usually the ones who built the most, sacrificed the most, and understand the business more intimately than anyone else alive.

Which is precisely the problem.

The Ownership Distortion

People overvalue what they own.

This is not opinion. It is one of the most replicated findings in behavioural economics. Show someone two identical objects — give them one — and they will consistently price the one they hold higher than the one they don't.

At mug-and-pen scale, the effect is small. At business-exit scale, after 20 or 30 years of personal investment, the distortion is enormous.

You don't see a company. You see the thing you built from nothing.

An acquirer doesn't see the thing you built from nothing. They see a set of future cash flows, discounted by risk.

Those are not the same lens. And they produce very different numbers.

Why Effort Inflates the Figure

The more painful the journey, the more valuable the destination must feel. This isn't a metaphor. It's a well-documented cognitive bias.

A founder who rescued a business from the edge — who put personal money in, who stayed when others left, who rebuilt after someone else's failure — carries a rescue premium in their head. The maths of what they went through demands a figure that honours it.

But the market doesn't price history. It prices the next five years.

It doesn't know about the sleepless months. It doesn't know about the funding gap you bridged. It doesn't know about the people you had to let go to keep the thing alive.

It knows the normalised earnings, the management dependency, the client concentration, and the sector outlook. That's it.

The gap between what the business cost you and what the market sees is not a negotiation failure. It is the predictable consequence of having built something with your life.

Why Familiarity Hides Fragility

There's a second distortion that compounds the first.

You know this business more intimately than any external observer ever could. You see the management team's capability. You see the client loyalty. You see the operational resilience built up over decades.

An acquirer sees something different. They see one owner carrying disproportionate relationships. They see a team that hasn't been tested without you. They see concentration that proximity has normalised.

This is not cynicism on their part. It's due diligence.

And the dissonance between what you see from the inside and what they see from the outside is where deals either stall or fall apart emotionally.

The Buyer's Chair

The simplest way to recalibrate is to sit in the buyer's seat.

If you were buying a business — any business, not yours — what would you pay for it?

You wouldn't pay for the history. You wouldn't pay for the turnaround. You wouldn't pay for the years of effort.

You'd pay for the profits. And then you'd discount those profits by every risk you could identify. Key-person dependency. Client concentration. Sector headwinds. Operational fragility.

The more you found, the less you'd pay.

That's not how buyers undervalue businesses. That's how businesses are valued.

The question this chapter leaves you with

"What would I pay for it — if none of the history were mine?"

Until that question is answered honestly, the premium you carry will either block the exit or poison the experience of completing one.

Chapter 5

The Value Gap (And Why It Feels Personal)

By now, three forces should be visible.

What you need — defined by your threat, lifestyle, and legacy thresholds.

What you expect — shaped by anchoring, comparison, effort, and ownership.

What the market will pay — indifferent to all of it.

These three forces rarely align. The space between them is the value gap. And the founder lives inside that gap for the entire duration of an exit.

Why the Gap Feels Like Failure

When the market offers a number below your expectation, it doesn't feel like pricing. It feels personal.

Because the business isn't just an asset. It's the central chapter of your life story. You built it. You carried it. You defined yourself through it.

When someone reduces that to a spreadsheet — normalised EBITDA, adjusted multiples, risk discount — the dissonance isn't financial. It's identity-level.

The question the founder is silently asking isn't "is this a fair price?"

It's "does this number validate what I've done with my life?"

No number can answer that question. But founders keep asking it of every offer that lands.

The Reframe

The value gap is not between what the business is worth and what the market will pay.

It's between who you are and what the market sees.

The market doesn't know your story. It doesn't care about your story. It prices future cash flows.

That's not cold. It's the mechanism.

Understanding the mechanism doesn't make it painless. But it does make it less personal. And making it less personal is the precondition for making a good decision.

How the Gap Shows Up

The founder who receives an offer that's technically sufficient but emotionally deflating — and can't explain why.

The one who rejects a fair offer because "it doesn't feel right" and then can't articulate what "right" would look like.

The one who delays selling because no number seems to match the magnitude of what they built.

The one who gets cold feet at the last minute — not because the deal is bad but because signing the paper makes the gap real.

These are not negotiation failures. They're the value gap expressing itself through behaviour.

Small Changes, Large Consequences

There is a structural reason why "roughly right" is never good enough in exit planning.

A 1% change in the assumed growth rate moves the sufficiency outcome by tens of thousands. A shift from cash-on-completion to a two-year earn-out changes the risk profile entirely. A different tax treatment can move the net proceeds by hundreds of thousands of pounds.

The value gap is not a fixed distance. It's a dynamic system, sensitive to initial conditions.

Which is why the work of defining sufficiency — as precisely as possible, personally, before the market gets involved — is what closes the gap. Not a bigger offer. Not a better negotiation. Clarity about what you need, separated cleanly from what you expect.

The question this chapter leaves you with

"Am I measuring this offer against what I need — or against who I think I am?"

That distinction is the difference between exits that feel right and exits that feel like loss, regardless of the number.

Chapter 6

Value Is Not a Single Number

Most founders think about value as a point on a line. Higher is better. Lower is worse. The goal is to push the number up.

But value in an exit is not one-dimensional. It exists across multiple axes — and two founders with identical businesses can rationally choose completely different positions.

Certainty vs Upside

A cash offer of four million today is not the same as an earn-out of six million over three years.

The headline is different. The certainty is different. The lived experience is completely different.

The founder with cash has liquidity. They can plan. They can act. They can stop thinking about it.

The founder with the earn-out has a bigger number on paper — and two years of dependency on an outcome they can no longer fully control. They've sold the business but haven't finished selling. They're neither in nor out.

The value of certainty does not appear on any spreadsheet. But it dominates how the exit actually feels.

Control vs Liquidity

Keeping the business means retaining control. You make the decisions. You influence outcomes. You know the levers.

Selling converts control into liquidity — money you can deploy anywhere, but can no longer steer.

Control feels safe because it's familiar. Liquidity feels dangerous because it's abstract.

But control in a declining energy state is a depreciating asset. The founder who is already mentally detaching, whose health is flagging, whose motivation has quietly leaked — their control is worth less with each year they hold it. The liquidity they'd receive by selling is worth more.

And control has a hidden cost that liquidity doesn't. It keeps you responsible. For the team. For the clients. For the decisions. For the outcomes. Every year of retained control is another year of carrying the weight — even when the weight has stopped feeling like purpose and started feeling like obligation.

Liquidity removes that weight. Not by eliminating risk — but by converting it from a form you carry alone into a form that can be shared, structured, and guided by others.

Speed vs Optimisation

Waiting another year might increase the multiple.

It might also increase the fatigue, the key-person risk, the chance of a market shift, and the probability of an earn-out rather than a clean break.

Speed has value — because time has risk.

A founder who sells six months earlier for a slightly lower price but exits cleanly, with full proceeds on completion, may be in a materially stronger position than the one who waited for the perfect number and ended up tied in for three years on deferred consideration.

The spreadsheet says one is better. The life says otherwise.

Earn-outs are rarely optimisation tools. They are often the price paid for carrying concentration too long.

The Satisficer's Advantage

There's a well-documented finding in decision science.

People who define a threshold and accept the first option that meets it — satisficers — are consistently more satisfied with their outcomes than people who keep searching for the best possible option — maximisers.

Even when the maximiser's objective outcome is better.

This applies directly to exits. The founder who defines their sufficiency number before going to market and accepts the first offer that clears it will almost always feel better than the one who keeps waiting for a higher bid.

Not because the first offer was better. Because the decision was made from clarity, not comparison.

The question this chapter leaves you with

"Which combination of certainty, control, speed, and price gives me the life I actually want — and am I willing to trade one for another?"

Value is not a point on a line. It's a position in space. And the right position depends on which axis matters most to you.

Chapter 7

Enough Is a Security Question, Not a Lifestyle Question

When founders say "enough," advisers hear lifestyle. Holidays. Houses. Cars. Monthly spending.

Those are valid inputs. They're just not what the founder is really asking.

What the founder is really asking is simpler — and heavier:

"When does this stop feeling dangerous?"

Why Lifestyle Is the Wrong Starting Point

Traditional planning begins with aspiration. How much do you want to spend? What does a good retirement look like? What's your target income?

These are useful questions — asked too early.

Because lifestyle only matters once threat has been neutralised.

A founder carrying concentrated risk doesn't lie awake thinking about holidays. They lie awake thinking about what happens if the business fails, the deal collapses, or their health gives out before the exit completes.

That isn't a lifestyle question. It's a survival question.

The Security Reframe

Every founder has a point — often unspoken — where exposure drops below the level that triggers constant vigilance.

Below it, decisions feel lighter. Sleep improves. Patience returns. Generosity becomes easier.

Above it, success never quite touches the sides. Goalposts keep moving. Risk feels omnipresent, even in strong years.

That point is not a lifestyle number. It's a risk sufficiency number. It answers: "In a bad version of the future, are we still okay?"

Why Lifestyle Drifts But Threat Doesn't

Lifestyle numbers are elastic. They shift with context, with peers, with aspiration. The holiday that felt extravagant five years ago now feels standard. The car that was a luxury is now a baseline. The spending level that once felt generous now feels tight.

Threat thresholds are anchored. They're driven by responsibility, dependants, health, age, and the irreversibility of the situation. They don't move with fashion. They move with life stage.

That's why one founder can feel calm on three million while another feels exposed on fifteen. The difference isn't ambition. It's where their threat threshold sits — and whether they've ever priced it.

Why the Chasing Never Stops

There's a neurochemical reason why founders keep pushing past sufficiency without recognising it.

The brain's reward system runs on prediction, not arrival. The anticipation of hitting a milestone releases more than the milestone itself. So the target moves. A million becomes two. Two becomes five. The finish line recedes at the speed you approach it.

This isn't greed. It's the architecture of goal-seeking escalation — and it's why founders who have objectively "enough" rarely feel it.

Defining sufficiency externally — through modelling, through structure, through a process that exists outside your own head — is the only reliable way to interrupt the loop.

The question this chapter leaves you with

"When does this stop feeling dangerous — and have I ever actually priced that?"

Until that's answered, no amount of optimisation will create peace of mind.

Chapter 8

Why Waiting for a Better Number Increases Risk

Most founders assume that waiting preserves options. It doesn't. It spends them.

The Decay Function

Value does not hold still while you wait. It requires energy to maintain.

When the founder's energy is declining — because they're over it, because their health is shifting, because the purpose has leaked out — the business begins to move toward disorder.

Not catastrophically. Gradually. In ways that are invisible until they're irreversible.

This is not a business failure. It's a physics problem.

Systems require energy input to maintain their current state. When the energy declines, the system decays. The rate of decay is determined by how much of the system depends on the founder — their relationships, their decision-making, their presence.

The more the business depends on you, the shorter its half-life without your full engagement.

The "One More Year" Loop

Once the psychological clock has started — once you've imagined the exit, pictured the clean break, begun mentally detaching — "one more year" stops being neutral.

It becomes twelve months of carrying responsibility you've already loosened internally. Twelve months of re-engaging emotionally after detachment has begun. Twelve months of staying sharp while motivation quietly drains.

Each repetition of "one more year" costs more than the last.

Not in business value. In cognitive capacity, emotional bandwidth, and the quality of every other decision you're trying to make at the same time.

The Unfinished Task

There's a specific psychological mechanism at work here.

Unfinished tasks occupy more mental space than completed ones. The exit that's been considered but not acted on sits in the mind like an open loop — consuming attention, creating low-grade anxiety, and reducing the bandwidth available for everything else.

The longer the loop stays open, the heavier it gets.

This is why founders in delayed exits often describe a feeling they can't quite name: not burnout, not fear, but a dull, persistent weight that colours everything.

That weight is not the business. It's the decision that hasn't been made.

The question this chapter leaves you with

"What is the cost — in energy, in health, in clarity, in the quality of every other decision I'm making — of carrying this open loop for another year?"

Waiting doesn't preserve optionality. It erodes the capacity to use it.

Chapter 9

Defining Your Number Before the Market Does

By now, one thing should be clear. Every question in this book leads to the same place.

Not "what is the business worth?" But "what does it need to be worth — for me?"

That number exists. It can be calculated. And until it is, every other question remains unanswerable.

What the Work Looks Like

The number doesn't begin with the business. It begins with the life.

What matters to you. What you want your time to look like. What rhythm makes you content. What your family needs — not in the abstract, but in monthly figures.

That becomes a spending requirement. The spending requirement becomes a capital need. The capital need, adjusted for tax, becomes the net figure you require from a sale. Add back the tax, the professional fees and the other deal costs and you arrive at the headline.

The headline is the last thing you calculate. Not the first.

Stress-Testing the Number

A single projection is not a plan.

Markets don't move in straight lines. Returns are not guaranteed. Inflation shifts. Tax rules change. Life intervenes.

The work is not to find a number that works in one scenario. It's to find a number that works across a range of them — and to understand, clearly, at what confidence level you can walk away and live with whatever the investment markets do next.

Some founders need to be 95% certain. Others are comfortable at 80%.

There is no correct answer. There is only the answer that lets you sleep.

What Changes When the Number Is Defined

Once sufficiency is defined, every subsequent decision simplifies.

Should I accept this offer? Measure it against the number. Should I wait another year? Model the risk against the number. Should I take the earn-out or the lower cash offer? Run both through the number.

The number doesn't eliminate complexity. But it gives every complex decision a reference point.

And a reference point — defined before the market arrives, grounded in your life rather than someone else's deal — is the difference between reacting to offers and evaluating them.

Founders who have done this work describe the same experience: a quiet confidence walking into conversations they used to dread. Not because the answer was always good news. Sometimes the number was higher than they expected. Sometimes it was lower. But in both cases, the clarity itself changed the quality of every decision that followed.

That is the point. Not the number. The clarity.

The question this chapter leaves you with

"Have I defined, precisely and personally, the number that means I can stop — and am I prepared to act when the market meets it?"

Until that work is done, every offer will feel like a guess. And every decision will carry more weight than it needs to.

Closing

Clarity Creates Leverage

This book has moved from one question to another.

From "how much is my business worth?"

To "what does it need to be worth, for me?"

That shift isn't semantic. It's structural.

A founder who enters a valuation discussion without knowing their sufficiency number is at the mercy of whatever the market says. A founder who enters knowing their number — what they need, what they're willing to trade, and what confidence level they require — holds the leverage.

Not because the market will pay more. But because the founder can make a decision from clarity instead of anxiety.

And a clear decision, made from a defined position, is almost always better than a reactive one made from a vague hope that the number will "feel right."

Enough — defined before the market defines it for you — is not a compromise.

It's leverage.

And the founder who holds leverage doesn't need to chase the biggest number.

They need to recognise the right one.

Ready to talk?

Most founders find a single conversation clarifies more than months of thinking alone.

No obligation. No pitch. We'll listen to where you are and tell you honestly whether we can help.
